Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI) is one of the most significant investor protection regulations introduced by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Effective since June 2020, Reg BI establishes a higher standard of conduct for broker-dealers and associated persons when making recommendations to retail customers, requiring them to act in the customer's best interest and not place their own financial interests ahead of those of the client.

In this Finance Dictionary episode from Financial Regulation Courses, we explain Regulation Best Interest, its purpose, the SEC's four core obligations, how Reg BI differs from previous suitability standards, and why it has become a cornerstone of modern broker-dealer regulation and investor protection.

Whether you're building a career in financial services, learning about U.S. securities regulation, or seeking to understand how financial professionals must serve retail investors, this guide provides a clear introduction to one of the most important regulatory developments in today's financial markets.

Key Concepts Covered
Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI)
SEC Regulation
Broker-Dealer Standards of Conduct
Retail Investor Protection
Disclosure Obligation
Care Obligation
Conflict of Interest Obligation
Compliance Obligation
Investment Recommendations
Securities Regulation
FINRA Member Firms
Financial Services Compliance

Regulation Best Interest strengthens investor protection by requiring broker-dealers to place the interests of retail customers at the centre of every securities recommendation. It represents a major evolution in the regulatory framework governing investment advice and remains essential knowledge for finance professionals, compliance officers, advisers, and anyone seeking to understand the U.S. securities industry.

metadata.title: Powered land for data centers: what "ready to build" really means
metadata.author: AECOM
metadata.shortDescription:
Join our Global Energy Markets Leader, Adrian Del Maestro, as he moderates an informative discussion with our data center experts and a special guest from Siemens on the critical importance of powered land (real estate with access to power to address data center deployment).
 
Topics included:
How to identify and evaluate powered land, assessing key criteria including power, water, fiber connectivity, transportation infrastructure and scalability.
How permitting, public perception and community engagement can impact project timelines and development success.
How AI and data-driven due diligence tools are transforming site assessment and investment decision-making.
What emerging power strategies, regional market opportunities and infrastructure trends mean for the future of data center development.

metadata.author: Industrial Real Estate Show
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode of the Industrial Real Estate Show, Chad Griffiths is joined by Matthew Smith, Vice President of RealNex. They look past the data center hype at what happens to these buildings, and the land under them, when the technology moves on. They cover what the midterm results could mean for new projects, why power is the real constraint, and who’s left holding the risk when a single-use building in the middle of nowhere goes dark.

- Why data centers cost roughly four times as much to build as standard industrial, around $800 a square foot versus $200, and why they’re so hard to convert back

- What happens to million-square-foot facilities in remote areas when they become obsolete, and why the land could fall from data-center premiums back to farmland value

- Why the tenant and the owner see the risk differently, and what investors should ask about decommissioning and remediation

Connect with Matthew: https://www.linkedin.com/in/matthewsmithca/
RealNex Website: https://www.realnex.com/


Connect with us: https://linktr.ee/industrialpodcast

metadata.title: How to Evaluate Land for Data Center Development • The Yield
metadata.author: Saunders Real Estate
metadata.shortDescription:
Data center development is changing how certain land assets are evaluated while influencing seller motivations. For landowners and investors, the question is not simply whether a property has acreage, frontage, or development potential. In most cases, the first question is whether the site can support the power and infrastructure demands that drive data center use. 

Tyler Davis, Spencer Smith, and Jerrod Parker discuss the unique value drivers behind data center development, including the role of power availability, transmission access, utility requirements, local policy, community response, and due diligence. The conversation offers a high-level look at how this rapidly evolving sector may shape opportunities for landowners, investors, and developers. 

Learn more at SaundersRealEstate.com.



ABOUT THE YIELD PODCAST
==============================================
Presented by Saunders Real Estate, The Yield draws on the voices of seasoned brokers and industry leaders to examine the forces shaping land and commercial property value. Through grounded, market-focused conversations, the podcast offers perspective on investment strategy, agricultural productivity, development trends, conservation, financing, land management, and the evolving decisions facing owners, operators, and investors.

And so for these data centers, right, if we're carrying personal information for people, you know, just like when you go to the hospital, they can't give that information out, you know, there's there's statutes that protect that. Illinois passed some statutes that keep that secured and require those data centers to go through some extra steps. Now, I think the concept of it was good, but it has tempered the ability for some of these developers and end users to want to come into the state. You're going to be an investor now, and all of a sudden I'm going to go reinvest. And so, that has helped keep some property values inflated a little bit. I'm not saying it's a five or 10% inflation from where we would be at standard market, but when you have a few of those buyers enter into that marketplace, it really keeps things propped up maybe for >> down effect of it. >> Yeah, yeah, there's just a little bit of a artificial inflation to the values. And so, your buyer profile, you know, gets a little bit not as deep, gets shallower. And so, that's something that I'm trying to keep an eye on >> Who loses in that situation? Local farmers wanting to go buy land to grow their their book, right? But if you're a landowner looking to exit, some of the state of center money flowing back in is a good thing. >> It's a trickle down effect, right? So, if I've been waiting to sell my property and I know that I've got extreme desirability because I've got somebody who needs to go spend $100 million in a short time period for 1031 tax deferred exchange purposes. And so, you know, you start thinking about that and the turnover ratios we have on land are so low historically because, you know, not everybody's willing to sell their land. I mean, it really does. And and it's I say that as a as a farm kid from Illinois who's very sentimentally attached, but at some point there becomes an economic threshold of, "Yeah, I'm willing to do that." And you own a site that seems to check a lot of boxes for data centers. I want to compare kind of that process of things they can be doing before engaging with a buyer or a developer. metadata.title: How to use Account-Based Marketing to drive enterprise sales | Bev Burgess
metadata.author: Growth Manifesto Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
This episode is a discussion about how to use account-based marketing to drive enterprise sales. So if you’re looking to increase the size of your B2B deals, then you’ll really like this episode.

SHOW NOTES

00:00:45 Bev Burgess’ introduction to the Growth Manifesto Podcast
00:01:59 How do you define Account-Based Marketing or ABM?
00:04:22 Where did the concept for ABM come from?
00:06:12 Bev expounds on how ABM aims to close the gap between sales and marketing and how everything is about client insight
00:08:11 What’s the difference between “Account-Based Marketing” and “Account-Based Engagement”
00:09:25 Who is Account-Based Marketing for?
00:11:33 What should companies take note of first before they start considering ABM?
00:15:01 Bev explains the different kinds of ABM
00:17:54 Where is the best place to begin to give yourself the best possible chance of a successful pilot ABM campaign?
00:20:39 Bev discusses the steps you need to take and how research always comes first when it comes to ABM
00:25:05 Is it better to start with an account you already have engagement with compared to starting cold in terms of ABM?
00:25:59 What would be the best way to start the ABM process with a cold account and how do you know you’ve picked the right company?
00:28:12 How do you conduct the research needed to have a higher chance of success in ABM?
00:36:53 What does the strategy and execution of ABM look like?
00:40:33 Bev talks about having a “surround sound” strategy when it comes to ABM where you cover both social advertising and social connection
00:46:17 Using personalisation, adaptive, and creative messaging to boost your ABM campaign
00:48:07 Bev discusses the best possible channels to do your research for your ABM campaign
00:52:16 How would you go about getting people to opt-in to your campaign so that you can start sending them something?
00:54:00 What are some of the coolest ABM campaigns you’ve seen?
00:57:02 Bev and Alex talk about how ABM is completely customer-centric
00:58:35 Where do you see Account-Based Marketing going in the future?
01:01:20 Bev talks about her book “Executive Engagement Strategies: How to Have Conversations and Develop Relationships that Build B2B Business“
01:03:23 How long should somebody test ABM for their organisation and start to expect a return on the campaign?
01:06:03 Quickfire Questions with Bev
01:08:17 What is one thing you’d like our listeners to do?

Subscribe to our channel to get new content as soon as it's released https://www.youtube.com/c/GrowthManifestoPodcast

metadata.title: How Strategic Gifting Drives Revenue Growth in ABM Campaigns | Outgage
metadata.author: AI Marketers Guild
metadata.shortDescription:
Can gifting really move the needle in B2B marketing? In this session, Mika Kayt (CEO & Founder of Outgage) and ABM expert Maggie Tonkin share how smart, personalized gifting campaigns are driving real revenue impact—far beyond one-off swag drops.

In this session, you’ll learn:

How to use gifting across the full marketing funnel—from awareness to retention

What makes a gifting campaign actually work (hint: it's all about follow-up and timing)

Real campaign results, including 35-97% engagement rates

How tools like Outgage help marketers scale without losing personalization

Cautionary tales (like chocolate gifts gone wrong…) and how to avoid them

*Get inspired with ideas you can test now—whether you're deep into ABM or just exploring new ways to reach your audience.

Brought to you by Serial Marketers and AI Marketers Guild.

metadata.title: Enterprise 1-1 ABM Play That Produced $1.3M in 40 Days
metadata.author: Steve Armenti
metadata.shortDescription:
Full walkthrough of our signal-based experiences program built for B2B SaaS marketing leaders running 1:1 ABM, enterprise ABM, and pipeline generation programs.

In this webinar, I break down how we use AI-powered research across 5M+ signals to study the human behind every title on your target account list, then orchestrates a real local experience around what they actually care about. 

It's not gifting. It's a 1:1 ABM play that proves you paid attention — and it's how we generated $1.3M in new pipeline from 30 contacts in 40 days.

What's covered in this walkthrough:

Why AI-generated outbound has broken cold email, LinkedIn outreach, and traditional ABM

How signal-based 1:1 ABM outperforms typical gifting platforms

The methodology: signal research → experience sourcing → moment orchestration

Pilot results: 11 booked meetings, $1.3M pipeline, 37% meeting rate vs. the 2–5% ABM benchmark

This kind of 1-1 is built for Demand Gen leaders, ABM managers, Field Marketing, Heads of Marketing, CMOs, and revenue leaders at Series B–D B2B SaaS companies running enterprise ABM, 1:1 ABM, target account programs, and pipeline generation campaigns.

If you're running ABM plays, account-based marketing, enterprise outbound, top-of-funnel pipeline, target account marketing, or any 1:1 ABM program — this is the new playbook.

Learn more or book a pilot conversation: 

https://twelfth.agency/

metadata.title: 5 ABM Campaigns to Land Bigger SaaS Clients
metadata.author: Rocket SaaS
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode, Ryan is joined again by Jess Chilman, Head of Growth at Rocket SaaS, to share five high-impact ABM campaign tactics designed to help SaaS businesses move upmarket and close six-figure enterprise deals. From research outreach to direct mail, podcasts, events, and bespoke campaigns, they explain how to build relationships with C-suite decision makers, stand out from the noise, and create memorable touchpoints that convert. If you want to move beyond mid-market clients and start landing enterprise logos, this is the playbook.

Takeaways:
Start with the BFG framework (Buyer, Firmographics, Geography) to build your high-intent account list
Validate your TAM and use intent signals (funding, hiring, leadership changes) to refine your ICP list
Campaign 1: Research outreach – co-create content with your ICP via surveys, interviews, or advisory boards
Campaign 2: Podcast ABM – invite C-suite decision makers as guests to build relationships and authority
Campaign 3: Events – run low-cost networking breakfasts or private dining sessions to connect face-to-face
Campaign 4: Direct mail – send thoughtful, personalized packages (chocolates, handwritten notes, themed gifts) to create standout moments
Campaign 5: Tailored ICP campaigns – design bespoke plays around your target’s pain points (e.g., mystery shopping, funding celebration gifts)
Align marketing and sales so every touchpoint has tight follow-up
These tactics work best together, creating multiple relationship-building touchpoints with decision makers

Timestamps: 
00:00 Intro: landing bigger SaaS clients
01:03 The 5 ABM campaigns for bigger deals
01:24 Building your target account list
04:37 What to do if you do not have enterprise CRM data
07:56 Using intent signals to find high-value accounts
13:26 How many accounts to target with ABM
14:20 Is your brand ready to move upmarket?
17:08 Campaign 1: research outreach
25:00 Campaign 2: podcast-led ABM
29:05 Campaign 3: small in-person events
40:10 Campaign 4: direct mail campaigns
45:11 Campaign 5: bespoke ICP campaigns
49:24 Why ABM campaigns work better together
50:49 Final thoughts

Join the SaaS Marketing Weekly Newsletter here: https://saasmarketingweekly.com/ 
Check out Ryan’s agency, Rocket SaaS, here: https://rocket-saas.io/ 
Send podcast guest pitches to: info@rocket-saas.io

metadata.title: ABM is a journey: How LiveRamp accelerated pipeline growth using a phased ABM rollout
metadata.author: Dun & Bradstreet
metadata.shortDescription:
Leverage account data, buyer insights and AI to create always-on personalized buying experiences.
It’s undeniable that Account Based Marketing (ABM) is the B2B strategy to implement in 2021 for organizations that want to ignite growth. However, while the B2B landscape continues to evolve, there isn’t much consensus in the industry around how to start and scale ABM. 
In this session, Andres Marquez, Sr. Portfolio Marketing Manager at Dun & Bradstreet and Ben Coffee, Director of Demand Generation at LiveRamp go over:
– Implementing a phased ABM rollout at your organization
– How LiveRamp 2Xed account reach, drove higher engagement and 4Xed MQL creation
– How to measure results and motivate adoption inside your organization

This discussion provides insights into account-based marketing strategies from Nick Bennett, Director of Evangelism at Alyce. Nick shares best practices for gifting, direct mail, and improving adoption of martech platforms. He outlines his role as an evangelist in martech and gives tips on building effective ABM programs. Additional topics covered include account acceleration tactics, multi-channel approaches, and customer retention strategies. Overall, the video offers useful perspectives on optimizing ABM and gifting campaigns.

metadata.title: How to Fit ABM in Your B2B Marketing Strategy
metadata.author: The B2B Playbook
metadata.shortDescription:
📖 Read the full breakdown: https://theb2bplaybook.com/account-based-marketing-examples

In this video, we break down account based marketing and whether it's actually the right play for every B2B business, or if you're better off with a broader approach.

We cover:
→ What ABM really is and why it goes beyond just marketing into sales and customer success
→ The three things you should consider before deciding if ABM is right for you
→ Why cataloging the market is the step most teams skip (and why it kills their ABM results)
→ How to run ABM alongside broader visibility ads without picking one or the other

If you are a B2B founder, marketer, or sales leader trying to figure out if ABM fits your business, or if you should just run it as part of a wider go to market motion, this episode is for you.

Tune in and learn:
✅ Why ABM might just be disciplined B2B marketing done right
✅ The deal size benchmark (around 10k a year upwards) where ABM starts paying off
✅ How to set objectives, define target lists, and tier your accounts properly
✅ Why cataloging contracts and timing beats spray and pray outbound every time
✅ When to run ABM and broader visibility ads at the same time

#331 | Dave is joined by a group of marketing leaders from Ramp, Snowflake, and Hightouch for a discussion about ABM and their plans for 2026. Casey Patterson (Director of ABM, Snowflake), Drew Pinta (Director of Growth Data Science, Ramp), and Brian Kotlyar (CMO, Hightouch) break down what ABM actually looks like in 2026 and what’s working right now inside of their companies. They share how they’re picking target accounts, aligning with sales, and building programs that go way beyond running ads. The group also digs into measurement, personalization, and how teams are using better data and AI to scale ABM without wasting budget. If you need a deeper dive on ABM tactics right now, this is the episode for you

metadata.title: Uniform Commercial Code Explained | UCC-1, Collateral & Real Estate
metadata.author: Applecation Lab
metadata.shortDescription:
The Uniform Commercial Code, or UCC, can show up in real estate when personal property is connected to a transaction or used as security for a loan.

In this video, we break down how the UCC works, why it matters in real estate, and how a UCC-1 financing statement can create notice of a security interest tied to personal property, fixtures, or collateral connected to land.

We’ll map out the difference between real property and personal property, explain what a security agreement does, and show why lenders may require UCC filings when removable fixtures or other personal property are part of the deal.

In this video, we cover:
• What the Uniform Commercial Code is
• How the UCC connects to real estate transactions
• Personal property vs. real property
• Security agreements and collateral
• What a UCC-1 financing statement does
• Why UCC filings may appear in a title report
• How lenders protect their interest in personal property or fixtures

Real estate concepts do not have to feel overwhelming. Let’s break the system down visually.

Disclaimer: This video is for educational purposes only and should not be considered legal, financial, lending, or real estate advice. Always refer to your state licensing materials, applicable laws, and qualified professionals for guidance.

🍏 Practice what you learned with The Applecation Lab Learning App: https://the-applecation-lab.lovable.app/

segments.text: Welcome to the application lab. Today we
are reviewing the uniform commercial
code. By the end of this lesson, you'll
understand what the UCCC is, how
financing statements work, and the key
details to remember for your real estate
exam. We'll cover a simple definition,
the UCCC1 financing statement, a real
world example, and finish up with an
exam tip and recap. Part one, a simple
definition. Let's start with the core
concept. Let's start with the basics.
The Uniform Commercial Code or UCCC for
short is a set of business laws created
back in the 1950s. Their main job is to
regulate financial contracts that deal
specifically with personal property.
Notice the focus there is strictly on
personal property, not the real estate
itself. Understanding this distinction
is key to protecting your investments as
a real estate professional or buyer. It
helps to separate personal property
rules from real estate rules. Personal
property items, think furniture or
specialized equipment, fall under the
UCCC when used as collateral for a loan.
Real estate operates under an entirely
different legal framework and is not
governed by the UCCC. Often personal
property gets mixed into real estate
transactions, maybe because it's
considered part of the property or
because it serves as security for a
loan. Knowing which legal framework
applies dictates the rules of the entire
transaction. The code itself has nine
articles and they each deal with
different aspects of banking and loans.
For context, 49 states have fully
adopted these nine articles of
standards. Louisiana is the sole
exception here. They've only adopted
article 3, which relates to negotiable
instruments like checks. It's a
fascinating quirk of the law that shows
just how state specific these adoptions
can vary. Part two, the UCC1 financing
statement. Let's see how lenders secure
this property. The UCC requires security
instruments to be properly documented
and this happens in three clear steps.
First, the borrower signs a security
agreement. This must include a complete
description of the personal property
used as collateral. Second, an
abbreviated version of the statement
called the UCCC1 or a financing
statement must be filed with recorder of
deeds. Finally, because the UCCC1
identifies the real estate involved,
this recordation pops up on a title
report. This step is vital because it
provides public notice to any
prospective buyers and lenders that
there's a recorded security interest
against the personal property tied to
that land. Part three, a realworld
example. Imagine a scenario where a
borrower pledges real estate as
collateral for a loan, but that specific
building includes valuable, readily
removable fixtures. We're talking about
things like custom chandeliers,
commercial refrigerators, or high-end
detached appliances. The lender needs a
reliable way to secure their interest in
those specific movable items completely
separate from the building itself. This
is where the UCCC1 filing steps in as a
safety net for the lender. The filed
document gives the lender the legal
right to confiscate the pledged personal
property in the event of a borrower
default. So if the borrower fails to

metadata.title: "Unsecured Business Loans" Financing Strategy Using A Ucc-1 Financial Statement
metadata.author: Business Credit America
metadata.shortDescription:
http://www.businesscreditamerica.com/ 1-888-883-3013

Interstate commercial transactions - such as contracts and loans - are governed by the Uniform Commercial Code, known as the UCC. 

All 50 states have adopted a version of the UCC. 

According to the UCC, when a lender secures a business loan with personal property rather than real estate the lender must file a UCC-1 financing statement with the Secretary of State's office. 

This puts the public and future lenders on notice that specific personal property of the business - such as equipment or inventory - is collateral for an already existing debt. 

The first lender to file a UCC -1 for specific property usually has priority over obtaining that property if the borrower defaults on the loan or files bankruptcy.

Filling a UCC-1 can  help build up the business credit rating of your business so you can achieve higher credit approvals once these documents are fully closed out. 

Business credit America can file a UCC-1 for five thousand dollars on behalf of your business. 

When choosing this package from Business Credit America you will also receive these three bonuses. 

You’ll receive a video that shows you the fastest and easiest way to get your Dun and Bradstreet Number in twenty four to forty eight hours instead of thirty days and without having to pay for it. 

We give a FREE Corporate Evaluation of your business.  This evaluation gives you an overview of what you need to do to help loan officer and investors take a serious look at your business model. This will help you get qualified for unsecured loans and investments.

you’ll receive the contacts to all of the micro lenders across the country.  With this powerful list alone, you can bypass traditional lenders and focus on dealing directly with lenders and investors that are interested in helping you make your business a success.

metadata.title: Let's Build Multi-Touch Attribution in HubSpot with Sarah Lane-Hawn
metadata.author: Value-First
metadata.shortDescription:
In this conversation, Chris Carolan and Sarah Lane-Hawn discuss the intricacies of multi-touch attribution, its importance in marketing operations, and the challenges faced in implementing effective attribution models. They explore the need for clear data integrity, the creation of a Goldilocks attribution model, and the significance of having a common language for reporting. The discussion emphasizes the importance of understanding limitations in data and the necessity of confidence in presenting data to executives. Sarah shares insights on how to navigate attribution within HubSpot and the strategic decisions involved in building or buying attribution solutions.

Takeaways

Attribution has become a buzzword in marketing.
Multi-touch attribution is essential for understanding omni-channel marketing.
Data integrity is crucial for effective attribution.
A simplified attribution model can be beneficial for small businesses.
Revenue attribution should roll up to 100% of total revenue.
Understanding the gaps in data is important for accurate reporting.
Confidence in data presentation is key for executive discussions.
Creating a common language for reporting helps in alignment.
Attribution models should be tailored to specific business needs.
Consultation can help in deciding between building or buying attribution solutions.

If your B2B SaaS agency cannot tie paid spend to closed-won revenue, you are flying blind on 73% of your marketing budget. Only 22% of B2B SaaS agencies run multi-touch attribution that connects ad spend to deal velocity, pipeline contribution, and CAC payback. The 6 US-based agencies in this video are the only ones we trust to deliver real revenue attribution, not last-click vanity dashboards.

We ranked 30+ agencies on 7 factors: attribution model maturity, HubSpot and Salesforce integration depth, GA4 and offline conversion expertise, MCP and live data pull capabilities, case study transparency, pricing, and platform certifications.

Revenue attribution in 2026 is the defining capability gap. iOS 17+ erased 38% of conversion data, GA4 still confuses 64% of marketers, and 67% of SaaS companies cannot answer "which campaign drove last quarter's closed-won."

Senior operators run attribution as a strategy lever. Junior managers ship dashboards. Senior operators reallocate the budget on the revenue signal.

So, the goal here is really simple, reduce uncertainty and increase commitment. The customer should come out of this evaluation period with more confidence that your solution works, and you should come out with more evidence that this is a real deal worth investing time into. Now, that takes us to the next stage, which is deal structure and negotiation. At this point, you've hopefully proven enough value that the conversation starts shifting from does this work to what would it actually look like to buy and implement this. And this is where you need to start getting really clear on the commercial structure of a deal. So, that means things like what are they buying, how much of it do they need, contract length, start dates, payment terms, implementation timelines, renewal structure, and then obviously price. And one of the biggest mistakes people make here is treating price like it's the only lever. I certainly made this mistake when I was new. A customer may care as much about other things like cash flow or payment timing or product flexibility or renewal protection as opposed to price. You also need to understand your own internal boundaries before you start getting into these conversations. So, what discount authority do you have at what bands, what needs manager approval, or what can and can't legal change, or implementation and support resources that would be available. You can't just be discovering this stuff while you're live and talking through it with the customer. You need to have a plan. And then just as importantly, you shouldn't be walking into a proposal or negotiation blind on the customer side either. So, this is another place where you can test your champion ahead of time before the formal evaluation, or excuse me, negotiation happens. So, ask them, what does the economic buyer, final signer, what do they care about? What concerns, if any, have been raised internally? What variables are going to matter most? Is it price? Is it contract length or start date? Flexibility, what is it? You want to start surfacing those things ahead of time so you're not hearing about them the first time when you're sitting across from the person who actually has final approval. And then when you do get into the commercial conversation, if they say this is too expensive, don't immediately start discounting. Ask questions like, compared to what? Or is it the total investment, the payment schedule, the scope, timing? You want to understand what the real objection is before you start giving anything away. And this is also where the give to get principle becomes very important. If you give something, you should get something in return, especially in a negotiation. So if you give a discount, maybe you get a longer contract term or a faster decision or better payment terms or a larger upfront commitment. The goal isn't to be difficult, it's to avoid negotiating against yourself and giving away value without getting anything back. And when you do present pricing, say the number confidently and stop talking. Don't immediately apologize or justify it or start discounting because there's a few seconds of silence. Just let them react and figure out what they actually care about. The goal here is really to get a commercial structure that works for both sides and protect the value that you have built and all that time and investment you made throughout the sales process. Now we get to the paper process and close. At this point, they may have decided they want to move forward, but that does not mean the deal is done. In B2B sales, there is a lot that has has to happen between them saying, "Yeah, I want to buy." and an actual contract getting signed. So depending on the company, that can include procurement, legal review, security questionnaires, privacy reviews or vendor onboarding checklist. There's so many things, contract redlines, and ultimately getting the right person to sign. And this is why you want to understand the buying process before you get to this stage at the very end. If the customer tells you, "I need to be live by January 1st, but legal takes 6 weeks and security takes another two." That changes the timeline. So, ideally you're asking questions earlier like, "Who needs to review the the agreement? Procurement, when do they need to get involved? Are there security requirements?" Ask all of those questions. And this is where also your joint execution plan becomes very valuable. Because if you already mapped out the remaining steps and who owns what and the target dates, you're not scrambling at the finish line trying to figure out what needs to happen here. Both sides should have a pretty clear idea of what's left and who owns each piece. Anyone who spent enough time in B2B sales knows that if something can go wrong, it probably will. Customers backtrack or priorities change or there's a new leadership transition. Don't underestimate a customer's ability to dis- disappoint you. So, you can't take anything for granted. Right up until the contract is executed, you should be looking for ways to reduce risk, confirm commitments, keep the right people engaged and on the right timeline so there are no surprises that sit underneath the surface or pop up. And that's why I don't want you to confuse intent with execution. We love it or we want to move forward. This looks great. They're all positive signals, but they're not the same thing as a signed agreement. Until that contract is executed, there are still things that can either delay or get in the way of your deal. So, the goal in this stage is to remove those final administrative and contractual blockers, keep the momentum going, and eliminate as much deal risk as possible.

metadata.title: Hybrid Lead Gen Model: Retainer Plus Pay Per Result
metadata.author: Rafael Hernandez ⚡️
metadata.shortDescription:
Big retainers scare clients off, but retainer plus pay per result doesn't. And most agencies waste every lead that doesn't fit their client's area or offer. That's money left on the table.

In this video, I break down the hybrid agency model. The client pays for the ads, and you run them from your own brand and your own ad account. They pay you a small retainer plus a bonus for every lead, call or appointment you deliver. Leads that don't fit get resold to other buyers, and you split that money with your client 50/50. Their half comes back as lead credits they spend with you, so every client grows your network.

In this video, you will learn:
✅ How to structure a retainer plus pay per result deal
✅ How to resell the leads that don't fit and split the money 50/50
✅ What to put in the contract: ad spend, data, pricing and credits

metadata.shortDescription:
Should your agency charge a rev share or a flat retainer? If a client will pay you performance, take it. If they won't, close them on a retainer. Every deal is different.

My Offers:

AI Assisted Agency - Build an AI Marketing Agency: https://go.clientascension.ai/?el=YouTube_DanielFazioHighlights_RetainerVsRevShareHowIWouldPriceAgencyClients&htrafficsource=YouTube

We show you:

- What to sell
- Who to sell it to
- How to get clients
- How to fulfill for those clients with AI

2. Olympia - (My Mastermind) Scale Your Offer with a Cold Traffic Offer and VSL Funnel: https://JoinOlympia.com/?el=YouTube_DanielFazioHighlights_RetainerVsRevShareHowIWouldPriceAgencyClients&htrafficsource=YouTube

This is for people already about $30k/mo. We help you:

- Build a cold traffic offer
- Build a VSL funnel
- Script, produce, and launch ads
- Sign 10-20 clients per week
- Build a sales team to close for you
- Build a fulfillment team to fulfill for you

3. 1-on-1 Consulting Calls with Me: https://danielfazio.io

4. All of my links here: https://linktr.ee/danielfazio

5. Follow my main channel: https://www.youtube.com/@danielfazio

A student of mine runs an e-com email marketing agency doing $18K a month with 8 clients, all from referrals. He charges a retainer plus a performance fee, and his pricing is all over the place. He asked me if that's sustainable, and whether he's charging too much or too little.

Here's the thing. You are not a SaaS company. When you run an agency, every single client ends up on a different deal construction, and it's messy. That's just how this business works. Pitch the performance deal first. If a specific lead won't take it, close them without the performance fee.

Then the part nobody tells you about performance-based pricing: the clients you'd want performance from are exactly the ones who won't give it to you. Agencies that charge performance usually pair it with an abnormally low retainer, so they end up stuck with clients who barely pay out. I will never give anyone a cut of my business, and I'm exactly who you'd want it from.

What you can charge also depends on your traffic source. Some people get 100% of their clients from content and referrals. A friend of mine sells base-plus-performance deals in-network at 8- and 9-figure founder events. If you're on cold email talking to ice-cold traffic, you can't command what they command.

So the price you charge is the price you can get them to pay. Look at their Klaviyo account, look at what they spend on ads, make the number up on the call, and negotiate from there. That's how retainer vs rev share actually works in a real agency.

00:00 Running An $18K/Month E-Com Email Agency On Referrals

00:59 Rev Share Plus Retainer: Am I Charging Too Little?

02:34 Why Every Agency Client Ends Up On A Different Deal

04:15 Why Agencies Stop Charging Performance Fees

05:14 Is Pricing A Skill Issue? It Depends On Your Traffic Source

06:13 You Charge Whatever You Can Get Them To Pay

It's a readiness and preparation conversation. It's a commercial value conversation more so than it's a sales conversation. There are a few pricing ideas that I want to share with you here. Idea number one. First the client is not buying your hours. They buy the result. There are two ways to price your work. Cost based, how many hours will this take me and what do I charge per hour? And value based, what is it worth to the person receiving it? Simple idea, completely different mindset. If you know you can move the needle on their revenue, on their margin, on their risk, on their growth, on their governance, that's what your price should be anchored to, not to your calendar and not to the hours it takes you to deliver. Idea number two, measure the value. In my discovery calls, I always ask if this works, what is it worth to the business over the next 12 months? I let them say the number. Sometimes the client might not be sure or they won't know. So your goal is to help them commercially picture the opportunity cost, which is what do they give up by choosing one thing over the next best [music] option? In this particular case is what it would cost them to not do anything and not to hire you. The revenue lost, the deals lost, the savings not achieved, the costs not optimized, the projects not delivered, staff turnover. Because once they named it and showed you the impact and then seeing your price as a fraction of that value you're going to provide them, it becomes a completely different conversation. Idea number three, if you show ours, they will negotiate ours. The moment a proposal has ours in it, the client does the maths, fee divided by the hours, and now you are not talking about the outcome anymore, you're not talking about the value, you're not anchoring your price against the value, but you are trying to defend your hourly rate. That's why the proposals that I review for my clients very often do not have hours involved in it. That's why [music] showing the hours in the proposal is not the goal. Idea number four, recommend an option, don't offer the menu. You're the expert, so look at their business, decide what they actually need, and propose that one arrangement with confidence. If they want to adjust, have that conversation live, but if the budget is lower, you change the scope, not the price. Never discount the same work because then the question will arise, how did you come up with that price in the first place if you've now discounted it so easily? Idea number five, price [music] from the value, then check it against two comparators. Work out the value that you create for them over the year, take 10 or 20% of that, that's your price. Of course, the bigger deals and the bigger wins will have a small percentage of your price attached to it, but generally it's roughly 10 to 20% of the value you're going to create. Then check the price against two things. First, [music] the market comparator. For example, what would it cost them to have the alternative, a full-time hire, an agency, or doing nothing? For example, if you do a fractional work, what it would cost them to hire a full-time person doing that work? Once you show that comparison and showing how much money you're going to save them makes the conversation much easier. Second, for your own purposes, compare the price you're going to charge them to the cost of what it takes you to do the work, but it's only for your internal purposes. Remember we spoke about, we don't show the hours, it's just for us to make sure we never lose the margin there. Now here is the psychology on your side. Most consultants I meet price like they're billing hours, not like someone who holds the outcome. If you find this video helpful, is this exactly the work I do with my clients. I help them close commercial gaps in their business models that prevents them from growing revenue, improving margins, and scale their consulting business without selling their soul by doing more hours. So if you wanted to look at your commercial gaps and your business, reach out at annaliman.com and we will go through business diagnostics and see what are the gaps that you potentially have in your business that I can help you close. So should every client be on a retainer? No. A retainer only works when the value is ongoing. Here is a filter that I use with my clients. A client needs to tick at least five of these six parameters before I suggest you move them to retainer. One, there is a recurring problem. It comes back every month or every quarter. Pipeline, pricing, governance, big decisions, commercial support. Two, measurable value. If you can name the impact, dollars gained, dollars saved, or risk avoided, this is a good [music] sign. Three, it's inside your mode. It's what you are unusually good at and what's known to be your expertise, not just some side random work you're taking because it pays well. Four, there is an outcome owner, a decision maker with budget who thinks I am paying for this every month, so I want to get the most out of it. Five, capacity to pay. The value is big enough that your fee at 10 20% of fraction of it makes sense to the company. Six, trust is already earned. You've delivered a project, a diagnostic or a quick win together, and now they're ready to move you to the retainer or potentially you've known them before. A pattern I see again and again is that the project opens the door and the retainer keeps it right. Let me give you some examples on what would work really well as a retainer and what would work well as a scope-based arrangement. For a HR consultant, a remuneration benchmarking review is the project, being their fractional people partner handling all the people issues as they come up is the retainer. For a PMO consultant, a program rescue is the project. Portfolio governance is the retainer. For a fractional marketer, the go-to market strategy is the project. Leading the launch and the pipeline is the retainer. So where the retainers do not work because I want you to leave the video knowing what works and what doesn't work for your model. metadata.title: The Best B2B SaaS Demand Gen Agencies for Pipeline (Not Leads) (2026)
metadata.author: GrowthSpree - AI Native B2B Marketing Agency
metadata.shortDescription:
Most demand gen agencies sell you leads. Cost per lead, MQL volume, a dashboard full of form fills that sales calls junk. Pipeline-first agencies optimize to cost per SQL, pipeline-to-spend, and cohort ROAS, and they feed your CRM signal back to the ad algorithms. Here are the ones that actually do it, and how to tell them apart.

In this video: why pipeline, not leads, is a measurement problem, how we ranked seven agencies, who each is best for, and five questions that expose a lead-gen shop.

The headline: lead-gen optimizes to form fills; pipeline-first optimizes to closed-won. Ask any agency what it optimizes to and whether it feeds CRM data back to bidding, and you will know which kind it is.

Sources: GrowthSpree agency rankings, 2026. This is our own list, and we rank ourselves first, with the rubric stated so you can judge it.

RESOURCES MENTIONED
Full Blog: https://www.growthspreeofficial.com/blogs/best-b2b-saas-demand-gen-agencies-pipeline-not-leads-2026

TIMESTAMPS
00:00 Pipeline not leads: the measurement problem
01:00 How we ranked them
02:00 The 7 agencies
02:45 5 questions to ask any agency
03:30 Which one fits your situation
04:00 Book your free audit

WHY PIPELINE NOT LEADS IS A MEASUREMENT PROBLEM
It is not a slogan; it is what the agency optimizes to. A lead-gen agency targets cost per lead and MQL volume, reports form fills on a 30-day window, and blames sales when they do not convert. A pipeline-first agency targets cost per SQL and pipeline-to-spend, sends CRM outcomes back to the ad platforms so bidding learns from real deals, and reads results on 90 to 365-day cohorts. Same ad account, completely different outcome.

HOW WE RANKED THEM
Two tests decide most of it: does the agency optimize to pipeline or to leads, and can it feed CRM signal back to bidding? Then we weight verified proof, B2B SaaS depth, aligned pricing, and dark-funnel readiness. Agencies that headline MQL volume, or cannot connect CRM outcomes to bidding, did not make the list.

THE 7 AGENCIES
1. GrowthSpree, pipeline-first demand gen at a flat fee. Best for B2B SaaS at 1M to 50M ARR that want cost-per-SQL measurement. Flat 3,000 dollars a month, no percentage of spend.
2. Refine Labs, brand-led demand creation. Best for 50M-plus ARR, 15 to 25K a month, impact in three to six months.
3. Powered by Search, SaaS-exclusive pipeline capture. Best for Series A to C, 10 to 20K a month.
4. Obility, B2B-only pipeline attribution. Best for 10M to 100M ARR with existing campaigns, 5 to 12K a month.
5. Wpromote, enterprise full-funnel across channels. Larger budgets with a media minimum, 10 to 20K a month, more e-commerce than SaaS.
6. Kalungi, fractional CMO leadership plus execution. Best for 0 to 5M ARR with no marketing team, 15 to 25K a month.
7. Single Grain, content-led multi-channel demand gen. Not SaaS-exclusive, 10 to 20K a month.

5 QUESTIONS TO ASK ANY AGENCY
Ask these on the first call. One, what is the single metric you optimize to? Two, how does our ad spend connect to the CRM pipeline? Three, your cost per SQL by channel for a recent client. Four, how do you measure the dark funnel? Five, when leads do not convert, whose problem is that? A pipeline-first agency answers all five. A lead-gen shop gets vague by question three.

KEY INSIGHT
Yes, we rank ourselves first, and here is the honest why. GrowthSpree is built for one thing: pipeline for B2B SaaS at a flat 3,000 dollars a month, no percentage of spend, so our incentive is your cost per SQL, not your ad budget. We feed CRM outcomes back to bidding through MCP and report on cohorts, not 30-day form fills. If you are 50M-plus and want brand-led demand creation, Refine Labs fits better. If you are pre-5M with no team, Kalungi fits better. Senior operators, 60M dollars-plus managed spend, Google and HubSpot Partner, 4.9 on G2. Cons: B2B SaaS only, not for B2C or ecommerce.

The takeaway: pick the agency by what it optimizes to, not what it promises. Pipeline-first means cost per SQL, CRM signal fed back to bidding, and cohort attribution. Ask the five questions, match the agency to your stage, and stop paying for junk leads.

ABOUT GROWTHSPREE
GrowthSpree is the #1 B2B SaaS marketing agency for pipeline, not leads. Senior operators (not junior account managers) who optimize to cost per SQL for B2B SaaS teams running $1K to $500K in monthly ad spend.

What makes us different: Senior operators only ($60M+ managed SaaS spend) · Flat $3,000/month · Google + HubSpot Partner · 4.9/5 G2 · Hyde Park, NY

Case studies: PriceLabs (0.7x to 2.5x ROAS), Trackxi (4x trials, 51% lower cost), Rocketlane (3.4x ROAS). Services: Performance, ABM, RevOps.

Not a fit for B2C or ecommerce.

Free audit: https://meetings.hubspot.com/ishan-m
Web: https://www.growthspreeofficial.com/

What trends are they focused on?" The

these are the kind of things that really

about it. Finally, remember, thought

the day, the more authentic and valuable

resonate, and the more likely it is to
attract the right people to your
network.

Both of these are traits of strong

Sharing your perspective not only

The more you understand your audience, the easier it is to create content that speaks directly to them. Thought leadership isn't about talking at people, it's about starting a conversation that matters to them. Next, focus on posting actionable insights, not just opinions. We've all seen posts that say things like, "Leadership is important." Okay, but why? And how do you actually apply that in the real world? To stand out, go deeper. Share your own experiences. For example, instead of saying, "Leadership is crucial," you could say, "Here's how I helped my team navigate a high-stakes project with tight deadlines and the three lessons that I learned." That shift from general advice to actionable insights that makes all the difference. It shows not just what you know, but how you applied it. Now, let's talk about hooks because the first line of your post needs to stop the scroll. A strong hook grabs attention right away. Start with a bold statement, a surprising trend, or a question that makes people really think. For instance, "Most executives think staying on top of the latest AI models is a priority. It isn't. Here's what actually matters most." That kind of hook makes people pause, it makes them think, and it makes them want to read more. And don't forget about the power of storytelling as well. Stories are what makes your content more relatable and memorable. Sharing your wins, your failures, and most importantly, the lessons that you've learned along the way, these are the kind of things that really help people to connect with real experiences that you've had. So, if you've overcome a major challenge or learned something the hard way, talk about it. Finally, remember, thought leadership isn't just about broadcasting your ideas, it's about starting conversations. But what if you're having writer's block or just don't have time to create a new post today? Here's the good news, you don't have to. One of the easiest ways to stay active and visible on LinkedIn is by engaging with content that's already out there. Here's how. Find influencers or other thought leaders in your industry and craft an intelligent, thoughtful response to one of their latest posts. This isn't just about leaving a generic comment like great post, it's about adding your perspective, asking a smart follow-up question, or even respectfully challenging a point that they made. Why does this work? Because LinkedIn's algorithm rewards engagement on the platform. When you comment on someone else's post, especially one that's already gaining traction, your response gets seen by a wider audience, including people in your target audience. So, even on days when you're short on time or feeling stuck for ideas, you can still stay visible and relevant by engaging thoughtfully with existing content out there. It's a simple, effective way to showcase your expertise without creating brand new content from scratch. At the end of the day, the more authentic and valuable your content is, the more it's going to resonate, and the more likely it is to attract the right people to your network. I get it. Sometimes staring at that blank LinkedIn post box feels like we're trying to write the next great novel. So, if you're stuck on what to post, here's a few simple prompts to help kickstart your thought leadership content. Start with common industry mistakes. Think about what's something that you see people in your field doing wrong all the time, or things that you've done wrong. Maybe it's a strategy that never works, or a mindset that's holding teams back. Share the mistake, and more importantly, explain how to fix it. A simple post like "One mistake I see leaders make all the time is this." can spark a ton of engagement. You might challenge outdated thinking as well. This one's great for starting conversations. Ask yourself, "What's an outdated belief in my field that needs to change?" Maybe it's a leadership style that no longer works, or common assumptions that are hurting innovation. Call out these ideas, get people thinking, get them commenting. And you can also share a hard-earned lesson learned. We all have those moments that we learned something the hard way. By sharing your mistakes and content that's relatable to people, it becomes more valuable. Think about a time when something didn't go as planned, and reflect on that. What did you take away from it? Try something like, "Early in my career, I made this mistake and it taught me this key lesson." We all have those lessons. By talking about these, you're showing both humility and sharing your wisdom. Both of these are traits of strong leaders. People also love speculating about the future and where industries are headed. So, ask what's the biggest challenge that my industry will face in the next 5 years? Or even where do I see the biggest opportunities emerging in the coming year? Sharing your perspective not only positions you as a forward-thinker, but it also invites your network to weigh in with their own thoughts and opinions. The goal here isn't perfection. It's sparking meaningful discussions that position you as a leader with valuable insights. And once you get started, coming up with new ideas gets a whole lot easier. You've crafted a professional resume. You've optimized your LinkedIn profile. And you've started sharing thought leadership content that highlights your expertise and set you apart. Now you're gaining some visibility and recruiters are starting to take notice and want to set up interviews. But here's the big question. Are you ready for those high-stakes conversations? In the next video, I'll show you the most effective way to prepare for senior-level interviews so you can confidently showcase your leadership value without spending hours on research. Click here now and let's make sure you leave a lasting first impression and secure that next interview opportunity.

metadata.title: From Expert to Impact: How to Build Real Thought Leadership on LinkedIn (Without the Fluff)
metadata.author: Impactable - B2B LinkedIn Ads Agency
metadata.shortDescription:
What actually is thought leadership—and how do you use it to drive inbound leads, trust, and sales?

In this first live session from Impactable, Justin Rowe (Founder & CMO) and Kayli Rela (Head of Content) break down how to scale authentic thought leadership across LinkedIn and paid channels.

They cover:
✅ What thought leadership really is (and what it’s not)
✅ How organic content builds trust and warms up deals
✅ Connecting your organic motion to paid LinkedIn Ads
✅ How thought leadership shortens sales cycles and improves close rates
✅ Practical tips for staying consistent without burning out
✅ Real examples of thought-leader ads, content batching, signal tracking, and retargeting

Whether you’re a founder, B2B marketer, or content strategist, this session gives you the blueprint to stand out in a sea of noise.

👉 Want to build your own thought leadership engine?
Check out our content offer: https://impactable.com/demand-gen

✅Watch our most recent videos: https://www.youtube.com/user/jrowe21am/videos

------------- Social --------------
Additional Resources/Guides/Courses  - https://linktr.ee/justin_rowe
Personal LinkedIn - https://www.linkedin.com/in/justin-rowe-4043339b/
Impactable Website - https://impactable.com/

Want to avoid getting burnt hiring a LinkedIn ghostwriter? Here are the key things to watch out for:

0:00 - The Reality of LinkedIn Thought Leadership
0:35 - Red Flag #1: The "No-Contact" Content Mill
1:28 - Red Flag #2: The Cheap Article Regurgitator
2:07 - Red Flag #3: The Executive Time-Suck
2:56 - Red Flag #4: Zero Niche Conviction
3:31 - The Perfect Ghostwriting Workflow

For more on how Social Hire approaches ghostwriting and turns your personal brand on LinkedIn into a source of new client wins, see:
https://social-hire.com/pricing-for-founders-partners-executives

segments.text: Building a personal brand on LinkedIn is
one of the most powerful moves a B2B
executive can make. But let's be honest,
you don't have 10 hours a week to sit
around writing posts, editing videos,
and designing PDFs. That's why hiring a
ghostwriter sounds like the perfect
solution. The problem is the market is
currently flooded with low-quality
writers who will completely dilute your
brand. In this video, I'd like to share
the four major red flags you need to
watch out for before hiring a LinkedIn
ghostwriter so you don't end up
publishing bland content that damages
your professional reputation. Red flag
number one, the ghostwriter expects to
produce your content without investing
any live one-on-one time with you. If a
writer tells you they can just look at
your website, read a few of your old
articles, and magically capture your
unique voice, they are selling you
short. To get real engagement on
LinkedIn, your content needs your actual
insights, your real-world anecdotes, and
your specific tone of voice. The
greatest success is achieved when a
ghostwriter periodically interviews you
and records the session. At Social Hire,
we do this via a recorded video call
because a single live session allows us
to extract content gold. We can turn
that one conversation into video
snippets, podcast clips, PDFs, polls,
and text-only posts. If a ghostwriter
doesn't want to get on a call to extract
your insights and expertise, they aren't
ghostwriting, they're just guessing. The
second red flag is the cheap writer who
mostly creates posts by sharing insights
from generic industry articles they
found on Google. Look, if your LinkedIn
feed is just a summary of news that
everyone in your industry already read,
you aren't a thought leader, you're a
news anchor. Cheap ghostwriters rely on
this because they don't have the
business acumen to push back or dig
deeper. Your audience doesn't want to
know what a journalist thinks about your
sector, they want to know what you
think. They want your contrarian takes,
your lessons from the trenches, and your
real-life stories. If the writer's pitch
is just I'll find articles and summarize
them, give them a miss. On the complete
flip side, red flag number three is a
ghostwriter who demands too much of your
time. The whole point of hiring a
professional is to buy your time back.
If your ghostwriter needs you to sit
through a 2-hour briefing every week,
approve endless drafts, and constantly
fix their mistakes, the productivity
gain of outsourcing is completely
destroyed. A highly efficient
ghostwriter only needs about a 45-minute
recording session every 6 weeks or so.
That's it. To complement that, a great
partner will just invite you to leave
quick WhatsApp or LinkedIn voice notes
whenever you step out of a great meeting
or finish a client call. You drop a
60-second voice note about a real-world
story, and the writer handles the rest.
If they take up more time than they
save, they are a bottleneck, not a
benefit. Finally, red flag number four,
the ghostwriter has never worked with
anyone in your specific line of work
before. B2B audiences are incredibly
sharp. They can spot a superficial,
generic post from a mile away. If your
ghostwriter doesn't understand the
nuances, the pain points, and the jargon
of your specific industry, the
conviction in their writing will be
compromised. The resulting posts will be
safe, bland, and easy to ignore. You
need a writer who already speaks the
language of your buyers, so they can
write with the authority that sparks
real comments and builds actual
pipeline. Your LinkedIn profile is your
digital shop window. Don't hand the keys
over to someone who is going to use AI
templates or generic Google searches to
represent your mind. Look for a partner
who values your time, interviews you
directly, and knows your industry inside
out. If you want to see how we manage
executive thought leadership the right
way at SocialHire, head over to the link
I've dropped in the description. Let's
get your true voice out there.

🚀  How We Can Help Double Your Agency's Productivity + Profits Using the ZenPilot System: https://www.zenpilot.com/working-with-zenpilot?utm_source=youtube.com&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=agency-journey-ep-299-garret-caudle
-----------------------------

"Managing a CEO's LinkedIn account is a full-time job."

Garret Caudle is the founder and CEO of Influent, a full-funnel LinkedIn marketing agency. With a background in scaling agencies and a passion for LinkedIn's untapped potential, Garret shares his expertise on leveraging the platform for thought leadership and business growth.

In this insightful episode of Agency Journey, Garret breaks down the strategy behind effective LinkedIn content creation for agency founders and executives. He emphasizes the importance of developing a clear point of view and consistently sharing valuable insights with your target audience.

Whether you're looking to establish yourself as an industry thought leader or generate more leads for your agency, this episode will give you plenty of inspiration and actionable advice to make LinkedIn a key pipeline driver for your business.

Episode Insights:
💡 Create a "thought leadership map" outlining your core beliefs and perspectives on industry trends. Use this as a foundation for your content strategy.
💡 Aim for 4 LinkedIn posts per week, focusing primarily on text-based content that showcases your unique point of view.
💡 Analyze engagement to ensure you're reaching your ideal customer profile (ICP), not just your existing network. Quality of engagement matters more than vanity metrics.
💡 Be patient - expect to see "green shoots" of results within 90 days, more consistent lead flow by 6 months, and significant impact by 1 year.
💡 Use proprietary data and unique insights from your client work to differentiate your content and showcase your expertise.
💡 Consider incorporating personal elements into your professional content to make it uniquely yours, without relying solely on selfies or personal anecdotes.
💡 Leverage your team's expertise by having them interview you about your POVs to generate content ideas.
💡 Write concisely and conversationally, leading with your main point or value proposition in each post.

metadata.title: Should You Hire a LinkedIn Ghostwriter in 2026?
metadata.author: Meet Sona
metadata.shortDescription:
Should you hire a LinkedIn ghostwriter? It depends on what you want out of the engagement, what your resources are and how much you want to spend.

In 2025, Edelman and LinkedIn's B2B Thought Leadership Impact report found that 65% of decision makers and hidden buyers prefer thought leadership content with a more informal and relatable tone. So whatever you pick, it has to come from you. It has to have you at the center of it or it is just not going to work.

Here is the short answer. A ghostwriter works if you have more money for a premium service, you want somebody dedicated to move you through the writing and you enjoy working with an actual person. An interview based system works if you have a little less budget, you are just getting started and you want a repeatable system with automation built in.

I have ghostwritten content myself and I ran an SEO and content strategy agency, so I have sat on both sides of this. I go through what each one really gives you, why these two are not even opposed to each other and the four questions to ask before you sign anything. Time commitment, price and payback, who is tracking your verbal identity and whether the process is actually scalable.

Key takeaways from Edelman/LinkedIn's third B2B thought leadership impact study.

Blog -- https://dsrghostwriting.com/theblog/edelmans-2020-b2b-thought-leadership-impact-study-key-findings/

Original report -- https://www.edelman.com/sites/g/files/aatuss191/files/2019-11/US%202020%20Edelman-LinkedIn%20Thought%20Leadership%20Study.pdf

For more information, visit DSR Ghostwriting at DSRGhostwriting.com.

metadata.title: Algolia × Pepper Case Study: Scaling SME-Led Technical Thought Leadership (Human-Led Ghostwriting)
metadata.author: Pepper - The Agentic Organic Growth Engine
metadata.shortDescription:
As the market shifted toward agentic AI, Algolia needed technical content that could keep pace—without compromising credibility or overloading their subject matter experts.

In this short case study, Neema (Head of Client Success at Pepper) shares how Pepper partnered with Algolia to scale SME-led thought leadership through a human-first ghostwriting workflow—turning expert insight into publish-ready technical narratives.

What you’ll learn:
- Why technical audiences quickly reject fluff (and “AI-spun” content)
- How we captured SME expertise with minimal time investment
- The workflow: focused SME calls → strong outlines → technically accurate drafts → tight iterations
- Why “thought partner” support matters when credibility is the bar

Featuring perspective from Tariq Khan, Director of Content Marketing at Algolia, on the value of human-centered creativity and credible storytelling for technical teams.

📌 Read the full case study: https://www.pepper.inc/case-study/algolia/
📩 Want a similar workflow for your SME content? Visit pepper.inc

#ContentMarketing #ThoughtLeadership #TechnicalContent #B2BMarketing #DeveloperMarketing #Ghostwriting #AgenticAI #Pepper
Linkedin: https://www.linkedin.com/company/peppercontent/
Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/pepper_content/
Twitter: https://twitter.com/Pepper_Content

#PepperContent

metadata.title: AskAVC #2 - SaaS Churn: what is it?
metadata.author: Ask a VC
metadata.shortDescription: One of the advantages of SaaS businesses is that you build a customer base that should not only continue to renew over time but also expand if you are delivering value. The opposite is the dreaded revenue churn. What is it and how to measure it is the topic of episode #2 of the #AskAVC channel. You can also check out the blog post based on this video, on my personal website - http://ryanfloyd.org/why-saas-startups-should-care-about-churn/.

segments.text: Hey everybody, Ryan Floyd, managing partner of Storm Ventures here with another video,
part of my video blog series on giving you some advice someone might give you
if I was an investor in your business or on your board or just what you'd like to hear from a venture investor.
Today, we're going to be talking about churn.
I've actually broken it into two part videos.
We'll first talk about churn, what is it,
and then the second part of the video series
we'll talk about what to do about it.
But today we'll talk about the dreaded, the dreaded churn.
You've worked so hard to get all these customers and then they leave and what do you do about it.
So let's get into churn.
So what is churn?
Well, churn simply put is loss of customer revenue.
Some people look at logo churn
and logo churn can be interesting in terms of loss of numbers of customers.
But really, when you look at what impacts your business, certainly in enterprise B2B businesses,
you're really looking at dollar churn in terms of what's really important to be looking at,
because there's probably going to be a variance in customers saying, look, if all customers are exactly
the same amount of revenue that they're paying you, then customer logo churn
and revenue churn will be virtually identical.
But in this case, we're going to be looking at dollar churn and why that's really important.
And the way to sort of think about it in SaaS is that it cuts both ways with these SaaS business models.
The good news is people sign up for subscription and you kind of get these annuity that pays over time,
so long as you're delivering value.
Obviously, the downside is, is if you fail to deliver that value, they have the ability to potentially leave
and with the cloud and APIs and people becoming much more digitally literate, it's getting easier and easier
for many people to decide to move on if they're not getting value out of what you're delivering.
First, let's talk about perspective,
the way to look at churn
is it's really your opportunity to improve.
Another magical thing about SaaS is this constant feedback loop where customers
can leave if they're not getting value.
So I tend to be kind of a glass half full kind of person and so the way I sort of think about churn,
is it's really your ability to improve, improve your processes, your product and everything you're doing
with your customers. And the reality is everybody has churn.
So don't fret because you're going to have periods of high churn and things are going to happen and it's OK
because it happens in every business. But come up from the perspective of, you know,
it's your opportunity to figure out how to do a better a better job in terms of selling.
So there's really, once you move on past logo churn, there's really two kinds of churn to really think about,
gross churn and net churn.
So gross churn is looking at your canceled business
against the ARR over that same period
in terms of what would come up for renewal.
And you might want to look at it over an annualized period over a longer period of time,
because you may only have had some contracts that came up for renewal in a given period,
so looking at monthly numbers, especially if you have a business where people are paying annually in advance,
doesn't make a whole lot of sense.
You need to sometimes look at it more in aggregate or an average number,
a trailing average, things like that.
Just think about really where your churn is headed.
But it's looking at, again, sort of what your overall business is canceling against what your ARR base is.
The other important metric in churn is to think about what's called net churn.
What's different about net churn is net churn takes into account the concept of not only your renewals,
your base, but also your expansion and then also any contractions that you might have had as well.
The reason this is important, especially with respect to the upsells, is that in any SaaS business,
really, one of the, again, things that's magical about SaaS is the compounding nature of SaaS.
And if you're not focused on churn, not only in terms of cancelations, but upsell,
it'll be very hard to grow.
And obviously, if you've got lots of customers that are canceling, it's pretty unlikely that you're going
to be driving a lot of upsell. So the two go usually very much hand in hand, not always,
but often very much hand in hand.
But it's important to look at them separately because if you have a lot of expansion in some accounts,
you may miss some of what the gross churn is as well and may present different issues to sort of look into.
So both numbers are important to be looking at.
So let's talk about really what is acceptable in terms of churn.
How do I really think about am I doing a good job?
Am I doing a bad job? Obviously, if you can drive your gross churn is zero,
that's where you want to head to.
It's unrealistic, nobody's perfect.
You're always going to have some customers that are going to churn.
Maybe they go out of business, you lose your champion, all these sorts of things.
They're going to happen from time to time and so an expectation of having zero gross churn,
is just simply unrealistic.

metadata.title: The NEW Way to Do Outbound Sales in 2026
metadata.author: Ronen Pessar
metadata.shortDescription:
Book a Call With Us: https://outboundoperators.com/

In this video, we break down why the traditional outbound playbook stopped working, what the new conversation-first model looks like, and how building your system around completed conversations instead of dial volume changes your CAC, rep productivity, and pipeline predictability.

Download "Outbound Sales, No Fluff" (Free): https://outboundoperators.com/resources

Follow Ronen on LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/rpessar/
Follow Ryan on LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/salesdevelopmentrepresentative/

If you found this helpful, subscribe for more!
