And that's the number that every other thing in the funnel should be working backwards from. Now, completion or a completed conversation isn't just any connect that happened on the phone. It's a specific thing. First, your rep reached the actual intended target, not a gatekeeper, not an AI assistant, and it's not an amount of talk time measured. The rep had an opportunity to cleanly deliver a concise pitch and most importantly, gathered information on where in the buying cycle this prospect is or if they're not even the right person. A completion will tell you after every call is complete, the system needs to know what is the next step. You schedule them for a future date. If it was a yes, you schedule them for a future meeting or have a sales rep call them back. Or you make a decision to try them back in the future or never. And maybe we try to nurture them through marketing. Basically, are we moving this prospect forward or are we moving them out? So, now the rep isn't sitting there at the end of the week wondering which of the 60 conversations actually meant something. Compare that to measuring dials, completed sequences, and even meeting set. None of those tell you anything about potential revenue or where your prospect is in their buying cycle. Dials just tell you how hard a rep worked, but they don't tell you if any work actually happened. Booked meetings are the most misunderstood [music] metric. All they tell you is your rep got someone to agree to schedule an interaction, but the industry standard is a 35% no-show rate. And then a good chunk of the ones that do happen go nowhere because the rep was incentivized to just book that meeting regardless of any qualification level. I've seen it all. And it's actually a lot worse than that. The real full picture cost of paying reps to set meetings usually turns that rep into a disrespectful, sleazy salesperson who's going to ignore everything a prospect says to them if it doesn't mean they're booking a meeting and the rep just pushes and pushes and pushes for a meeting, which ultimately just poisons the well with bad behavior one call at a time. A completion can't be faked or forced because you either had a real conversation and understood what the prospect's response was to your pitch or you didn't. [music] It's a data point. It's a signal and it's an outcome. Now, the target that you want to build towards on this model is going to be somewhere between 15 [music] to 20, maybe 25 completions per rep per day. Now, that's the benchmark we see on teams running this new model and it's a 15 to 25x increase from what most teams are able to produce right now, which is maybe zero, one, or two conversations per rep per day. Once you hit that volume of real connects and completions, your pipeline starts to become powerfully predictive. You will see exactly what percentage of your market is working with competition, what percentage is a no now but maybe later, which is a really great signal, [music] and you're going to see what's driving results not just for today, but for the next two to six [music] weeks. And you're going to see what's driving today's results as well as the next three months of potential results. It also means that one rep running inside of the system will roughly produce the same outcome of a team of six to 10 inside the old [music] one, which will completely change how you think about building your outbound team. Now, the first thing that's going to change is outbound will become phone first again. Simply because the phone is actually now scalable and the economics will work as you grow it. When you have the right rep hitting calls with a clean caller ID, calling phone numbers from a scored list, that rep can hit 16 to 40% connect rate, one conversation every two to five dials, which means that every day that rep can have somewhere between 25 and 40 connects, which is exactly what you want your whole outbound team hitting. Now, before any rep starts dialing, every phone number you pull from a database has to first get scored for its reachability or phone intent. My partner Ryan built and sold a company called Phone Ready Leads, which is now called TitanX. This is exactly what they do. They take your phone numbers and score them for likelihood to pick up. This basically tells you if a person will answer the phone when you call them or not. The numbers that don't get answered don't go to a rep. And the ones that do get prioritized for a rep to go call. This way the reps efficiently spend their time with people who are actually going to answer. Last quarter, for example, we took one of our clients' existing list of about 2,245 numbers, and we re-scored it and then went to go call it in our proof of concept, our outbound go-to-market readiness assessment. That list went from one conversation every 60 dials to 21 conversations from 53 dials. That's roughly a 23x lift in dial-to-connect. Or said differently, it was about a 39.6% dial-to-connect rate instead of what would have been a 1.6% dial-to-connect rate. At 60 dials a day, that would have been an entire month's worth of conversations in 2 hours of dialing off of the exact same list that they were already going to work without adding a single new prospect to the list. The second critical part of the system is follow-up because people who pick up the phone once will pick up the phone again and again and again. When someone answers a cold call, even if it's just a 10-second exchange, they now enter what we call a priority bucket or priority status, which is a list of contacts who have proven that they will engage on the phone. Now, >> [laughter] >> most reps treat a short call like that as a dead end. But when you start running outbound this way, it's the single most valuable follow-up task that you have. Because when I go call that person back in the future and have another conversation, we typically see that 20 to 40% of those convert to the next step simply by calling them back and having another conversation. Now, when you put them together, the right rep dialer, calling lists that have been scored, and a follow-up system, and of course the right script, too, your whole unit economics for outbound changes dramatically. One rep running inside of this new system will produce the same outcomes, if not more, than a team of six to 10 in the old system. This is what we saw firsthand with management controls. They had four, and then eventually three reps on the team that hit 106% of a full-year pipeline target halfway through the year at the halfway mark. And that was against their original plan that said they would have needed 34 reps. And they achieved that with a team of four. Obviously, that means your cost of acquisition is coming down, because you're paying for way less headcount and way less software to produce the same pipeline, [music] and often more pipeline. But here's the real catch is the conversations happen [music] way quicker. You're going to condense time in the new system. What used to take 6 months will now take 2 weeks. And it means that new reps are productive on day one and two, fully ramped within their first month, instead of being fully ramped somewhere between month three and six. Because the list is doing a lot of the work that used to fall on how skilled a rep was. And obviously, when a new rep is having 25 to 40 connects a day, instead of one or two, they learn a whole lot faster. So, outbound still works, but the version most companies are running right now is just built for a time when the phone, emails, and LinkedIn all worked the way it used to. This new way doesn't require a bigger team, better reps, more software. It actually requires fewer reps, less software, and a simplified system. Building the system around the thing that actually predicts revenue, which is completions. I reached the right prospect, we had a conversation, and I can document exactly what and why their outcome was what it was. So, look, if you want to see how this new way of doing outbound could work in your organization, click the first link in the description and book a call with us. On that call, we'll show you exactly how this works, and we'll even call your prospects. So, by the end of it, you'll know if your organization can even support outbound in this new way and if so, what it would take. You'll also know what your list reaches, how many people ever pick up the phone, if your message is resonating with your audience, what your conversion math is, >> [music] >> your projected cost of acquisition and ROI from the phone, and most importantly, what the right team size is [music] to support your revenue goals. We've done this already for dozens of organizations and we'd love to see how we can help you as well. The call is free, so again, in the description, you'll find a link where you can book the call. And if you want to see how we replaced 34 SDRs with just four and beat the pipeline goal, then check out this video next.

metadata.title: How Government Contractors Find Teaming Partners in the Federal Market
metadata.author: Neil McDonnell
metadata.shortDescription:
Government contractors significantly increase their revenue options by teaming with other small businesses and large prime contractors.
✅   In this training, Neil McDonnell explains :
👉   What is teaming and why is it a good idea?
👉   Using a Teaming Partner Worksheet to find the right teaming partners
👉   Teaming Partner Criteria (10 suggestions)
👉   Top Tips for building a strong Government Contracting Team

✅   TEAMING gives you access to:
•  closed opportunities​ 
•  set-aside awards (e.g., 8(a), WOSB, Veteran-Owned, HUBZone etc)​ and 
•  GSA  Contract Vehicles (e.g., OASIS, STARS III)​
• diverse pool of  Technical Expertise (access to SMEs)​

✅   RELATED TRAINING

metadata.title: State Farm Roof Memo: Why Hail Claims Get Denied
metadata.author: Policy & Property
metadata.shortDescription:
State Farm roof claim denied after hail? An internal State Farm memo made public in an Oklahoma lawsuit this week shows how wind and hail roof claims were measured, and why the repair-vs-replace call and your deductible decide whether a hail damage insurance claim pays anything.

We cover "Exhibit 133" in Hursh v. State Farm (ruled not privileged Oct 26, 2026): the January 2021 rule requiring manager approval for full roof replacements on small hail and light wind, the drop in full replacements (3.21:1 to 1.95:1 vs partial repairs), closed-without-payment ratios near 39, State Farm's denial, the Dec 7 trial date, and the math: on a $300,000 home with a 2% wind/hail deductible, the same storm can pay $0, $1,800 or $9,000. Plus 8 steps if your roof claim is denied or underpaid.

Chapters:
0:00 State Farm's roof memo made public
0:55 What the memo says
3:35 How a roof claim becomes $0
4:38 The deductible math (3 outcomes)
6:41 8 steps if you're denied
8:32 What it means for your next policy
9:18 Takeaway

Sources:
- The Oklahoman (via Wichita Eagle), State Farm warned internally about cutting payouts, Oct 30, 2026: https://www.kansas.com/news/nation-world/national/article317846288.html
- Allied Emergency Services News, Exhibit 133 ruling and full quotes, Oct 29, 2026: https://www.news.alliedemergencyservices.com/state-farm-exhibit-133-roof-memo-not-privileged/
- KFOR via Yahoo News, Oct 29, 2026: https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/attorneys-state-farm-document-reveals-225100664.html
- Angi 2026 roof replacement cost ($9,610 avg): https://www.angi.com/articles/how-much-does-roof-replacement-cost.htm
- Angi 2026 shingle repair cost ($960 avg): https://www.angi.com/articles/cost-to-repair-asphalt-shingles.htm
- The Roofing Brief 2026 cost report (Verisk $17,631 avg): https://theroofingbrief.com/2026-roofing-cost-report

Allegations in the lawsuit are disputed by State Farm and have not been decided by a court. Dana's numbers are an illustration; your policy, deductible and roof will differ.

Education only, not financial/insurance advice. AI narration: the narrator is an AI voice. Policy & Property is not a licensed insurance agent, adjuster or attorney.

If this helped, please LIKE, COMMENT (have you ever had a roof claim denied?), SHARE with a homeowner, and SUBSCRIBE: https://www.youtube.com/@PolicyAndProperty
Related: Home Insurance Rates 2026: Why They Keep Rising: https://youtu.be/LjR-g7_m2PE
#StateFarm #RoofClaim #HailDamage #HomeInsurance

segments.text: A hailstorm hits your street.
Your neighbor gets a brand new roof.
You get a letter saying your claim is
closed with $0 paid.
This week, a court in Oklahoma made
public an internal State Farm memo about
exactly that kind of claim.
In it, one of State Farm's own reviewers
warned the numbers could look like the
company was, {quote} intentionally
reducing what it paid.
State Farm denies doing anything wrong,
and nothing has been proven in court.
But the memo is a rare look inside how
roof claims get decided.
Stick around, because in a few minutes
I'll show you the one number on your
policy that decides whether a roof claim
pays anything at all.
This is Policy and Property, where we
turn insurance and housing news into
decisions.
Education only, not advice, and the
narration is an AI voice.
Part one.
What exactly came out this week?
The case is Hirsch versus State Farm,
filed by an Oklahoma couple and treated
as a test case for how wind and hail
claims were handled.
The law firm behind it says it
represents nearly 1,000 homeowners
making similar claims against the
insurer.
The document is a summary written for
State Farm senior executive offsite in
October 2021, titled Fire Claims, Roofs,
Quality, and Service.
On October 26th, Oklahoma County Judge
Amy Palumbo ruled it was not protected
by attorney-client privilege and denied
State Farm's request to pause that
ruling.
So, what does it actually say?
Start with the rule change at the center
of it.
Starting in January 2021, after a
6-month run in Texas, a full roof
replacement on claims from small hail or
light wind needed a team manager's
approval.
Next to that line, a reviewer wrote,
"Caution, our adversaries could say this
places pressure on frontline claim reps
to not replace a roof.
Then come the results.
Before the change, State Farm replaced
about 3.2 roofs fully for everyone it
repaired.
After the change, that fell to about two
to one.
That's roughly a 40% drop in full
replacements relative to repairs.
And the share of claims closed without
any payment went up.
Wind claims rose 17 points to a ratio of
Hail rose 13 points to 39.3.
The homeowner's lawyers read that as
nearly four in 10 claims closing without
a dime.
The reviewer flagged that, too. Does
this suggest closing claims without
payment is an improvement?
The memo also compared State Farm to the
industry.
In Texas, it had paid full roofs on 90%
of moderate hail claims.
An outside benchmark it cited put the
industry's best at 5 to 10%.
In other words, the goal looked like
replacing far fewer roofs.
The in-house reviewer pushed back on
that framing, writing that quality
should not be measured by reducing the
number of roof replacements.
State Farm's position is that this was
an honest review aimed at accuracy, and
that the comments were its lawyers'
advice about wording.
It told the Oklahoman the plaintiff's
claims are false, and it never tries to
arbitrarily cut roof replacements.
The trial is set for December 7th.
Part two.
Forget the lawsuit for a second.
Here's how any roof claim, with any
insurer, can end at $0.
When an adjuster inspects hail damage,
the biggest decision is not whether
there's damage.
It's whether you get a repair or a full
replacement.
A typical shingle repair costs around
according to Angie's 2026 data.
A full roof replacement averages about
$9,600 on Angie and closer to $17,600
in Verisk data.
Now add the piece most homeowners
forget, the wind and hail deductible.
In many states, it's a percentage of
your home's insured value, not a flat
amount.
On a home insured for $300,000,
a 2% deductible is $6,000 out of your
pocket first.
Here's the trap.
If the adjuster writes it up as a
repair, the estimate can land below your
deductible.
Part three,
the math with one example homeowner.
Let's call her Dana in Oklahoma City.
Dana's home is insured for $300,000
with a 2% wind and hail deductible.
Her roof is 12 years old.
Outcome A,
the adjuster sees scattered damage and
writes a $2,500 repair.
Subtract her $6,000 deductible.
The insurer pays nothing.
On paper, that's a claim closed without
payment, even though there was real
damage.
Outcome B,
a different call, full replacement at
which is inside the range the 2026 cost
data shows.
Subtract the same $6,000 deductible.
Now the insurer pays $9,000.
Same storm, same roof, a $9,000
difference from one judgment call.
Outcome C is where many policies quietly
differ, actual cash value.
Instead of paying what a new roof costs,
they pay what your old roof was worth.
Say Dana's 12-year-old roof was built to
last about 25 years.
That's 48% used up, so $7,200 of
depreciation comes off.
Then the $6,000 deductible.
The check is $1,800.
On an older roof, an ACV policy can turn
a $15,000 job into a small check.
Put the three side by side.
The same hail storm can pay zero, 1,800,
That's why the repair versus replace
call and your deductible type matter far
more than most people think when they
buy a policy.
Quick pause.
If you've ever had a roof claim denied
or underpaid, tell me in the comments
what your insurer said.
I read them.
Part four.
Eight steps if your roof claim is denied
or comes in low.
These work with any insurer in any
state.
One.
Pull your declarations page tonight.
Find your wind and hail deductible and
whether your roof is paid at replacement
cost or actual cash value.
Two.
Document everything right after the
storm.
Dated photos of shingles, gutters,
vents, siding, and soft metals like
downspouts.
Three.
Be home for the adjuster's inspection
and ask them to show you what they
marked and what they ruled out.
Four.
Ask for the written estimate and the
reason for any denial in writing.
You need the exact wording to challenge
it.
Five.
Get a written estimate from a licensed,
reputable roofer.
The memo itself noted agents saying
reputable contractors disagreed with
some damage findings.
Six.
Ask for a reinspection and if an
engineer was used, request a copy of the
engineer's report.
Seven.
If you disagree only on the amount, many
policies have an appraisal clause where
each side picks an appraiser and an
umpire settles it.
Eight.
File a complaint with your state
insurance department.
Every state has rules against unfair
claim practices and complaints are
tracked.
And watch the clock.
Policies set deadlines to file a claim
and to sue, so check yours before a
delay costs you the right to argue.
For a big claim, a licensed public
adjuster or an attorney may be worth it.
Public adjusters usually take a
percentage of the payout, so ask the fee
up front.
Part five.
What this means for your next policy,
even if you never file a claim.
When you compare quotes, compare the
wind and hail deductible, not just the
premium.
A cheap policy with a 5% deductible can
cost you more.
Ask directly whether your roof is
covered at replacement cost or on a
depreciation schedule once it reaches a
certain age.
If you're replacing a roof anyway, ask
about discounts for impact resistant
shingles.
Some insurers and states offer them.
State Farm's lawyers argue that each
claim should be judged on its own file.
The homeowners say the memo shows a
pattern.
A jury may decide in December.
Either way, the lesson is the same.
Know your deductible, document
everything, and don't treat the first
answer as the final one.
If this helped, hit like and comment.
Should a manager have to approve a roof
replacement, but not a denial?
Share it with a homeowner who needs it
and subscribe for more.
Like, comment, share, and subscribe to
Policy and Property.
See you in the next one.

metadata.title: Commercial Roof Hail Damage: Is It Really Cosmetic?
metadata.author: Merlin Law Group
metadata.shortDescription:
Was your commercial roof hail claim denied or reduced because the insurer called the damage “cosmetic”? Chip Merlin explains why a dent’s appearance may not tell the whole story—and why your policy’s exact wording matters.

For commercial policyholders, public adjusters, and damage contractors, this video covers:

• Cosmetic damage versus functional roof damage
• Why hail impacts may affect underlayment or roof lifespan
• How cosmetic damage exclusions can affect a claim
• Why professional investigation and legal advice may be needed in a coverage dispute

The condition of the roof and the terms of the policy matter. Calling damage “cosmetic” does not resolve those questions by itself.

Learn more about hail damage claims:
https://www.merlinlawgroup.com/types-of-loss/hail-damage/

Subscribe to Merlin Law Group for more on commercial property insurance claims and policyholder rights.

This video provides general information, not legal advice. Coverage depends on the policy language and facts of the loss.

#HailDamage #CommercialRoofing #InsuranceClaims

segments.text: If you're a policy holder, and whether
it's a commercial policy or a
residential policy, and you had a hail
storm that damaged your structure, and
the insurance company calls back and
says, "All of your damage is cosmetic in
nature, and we're not going to pay for
the full amount. We're not going to pay
for the loss at all." The insurance
company's essentially arguing this, and
that is that the damage, the physical
alteration, had nothing to do with the
function of the roof. It got damaged a
little bit. There's a dent here, but it
doesn't impact at all the life ex
pectancy of it. It's not going to
prevent the water penetration from
later. All it's going to do is just to
look a little bit aesthetically
displeasing. And this is where policy
holders need to go back and actually do
a better investigation. The truth is
many impacts by hail, while they might

The CFO feels the cost of inefficiency, the VP of sales feels the lost revenue, and the person doing the work every day just feels the frustration. Your job is to name the problem so precisely that a prospect recognizes it instantly. And this lesson gives you three lenses for that. The job your product is hired to do, the business outcome it creates, and what's personally at stake for the buyer. First, a customer buys a solution to a problem, not a product. So, define the problem before anything else. Second, different stakeholders in the same company experience that problem differently, and your ICP has to account for that. Third, your product solves a job to be done, but it also creates a business outcome and carries personal stakes for whoever's buying it. Fourth, problem definition isn't something you do once and file away. It's iterative. And maybe most importantly, a clearly defined problem is the foundation everything else in your ICP gets built on. The first is jobs to be done, originally from Clayton Christensen. It pushes you past demographics to the functional, social, and emotional needs a customer is really hiring your product to satisfy. The job they need done, not the features they're buying. Use it to frame your entire ICP around the customer's actual goal, not your product category. The second is the three value frameworks, and its job is making sure you understand and communicate value to every stakeholder, not just one. It sorts the value you provide into three buckets: functional value, like saving time, business value, like increasing revenue, and personal value, like reducing someone's anxiety. Map your problem against all three, and you'll know exactly what to say to each different person in the room. The quality of your ideal customer profile comes down to how clearly you can name the problem you solve. Most B2B companies define themselves by their product category instead of the business crisis they actually fix, and this lesson forces you out of that habit. You're going to write the problem the way your customer would say it, not the way your internal deck describes it. Honest work here means ditching the jargon and writing in the language people actually use when they're in pain. The shortcut version is a vague sentence full of buzzwords that could describe anyone. By the end of this lesson, the output is your problem statement, a concise, powerful sentence that names the pain you alleviate. Take it seriously. Everything downstream in this workbook is built on top of that one sentence. So, rushing it now means your team feels the consequences for months. Grab your workbook. Printed or in your own notes works, too, since what matters is that you actually write these down. First, pull up your sales call notes, support tickets, and insurance surveys, and list the top three business problems your customers were facing right before they bought. Write them the way the customer said them, in their words, not yours. Something like, "We were losing hours every week reconciling data between Salesforce and our marketing system, and it was causing reporting delays." Pause and get all three down before moving on. Next, look at that list and ask which one is the most urgent, painful, and expensive for your best customers. The one that, solved, makes you indispensable. That becomes your single core problem statement. This is the sentence everything else in this workbook gets built from, so don't rush it. Finally, take that core problem and write down how it lands differently on the C-suite, the department head, and the end user. That cascade is what shows you the problem isn't one flat thing. It hits different people in different ways, which is exactly what you'll need when you map stakeholders. Here's your checklist for this lesson. List your top three customer problems in their own words. Refine the most urgent one into a single core statement. Write three sentences on how it hits the C-suite, department head, and end user. Review the jobs to be done and three value frameworks material, and share your core problem statement with one sales colleague for a gut check. Together, these produce your first real deliverable, a validated core problem statement. It's not just a phrase. It's a shared understanding your whole team can point to, and it's what the next lesson stakeholder mapping is built from. ----------------
Before you select the persona and the ideal customer profile, take time to understand the broader audience. This knowledge will help you select the optimal customer segment to target and even select personas whose attitudes, values, and beliefs align with your organization. 

Here are the steps to build a more comprehensive view of your customers.

1) Understand the larger target audience that might have the pain that you are solving. For example, your target audience can be all VPs of Sales regardless of the size of organization or industry. The fact that people experience the same pains doesn't mean that they have identical context. 

2) Identify potential customers (people who have a particular problem that your product solves) out of the larger target audience 

3) Build an ideal customer profile (ICP). 
These prospects do not only have pain and are a good fit but also are ready, willing, and able to buy your product. Ideally, the person who fits your ICP is aware of the problem and already looking for a solution to it. 

4) Create customer personas. 
And only then, after we understand the larger target audience and their environment, and then outlined the primary target in the form of an ICP, can we dig into the psychographic and personality threads — attitudes, beliefs, values, etc. — of your customers

Learn more about lead generation with Hunter: 
- Build buyer personas: https://youtu.be/po6YQuA_844 
- Writing a great outreach email: https://youtu.be/1tL1yGqXB-A 
- Improve your email deliverability: https://youtu.be/4CIPqHS8et0 
- 6 things to stop doing in email outreach: https://youtu.be/Qn8vGrUKKvY

Most skip the single most important step in lead generation — defining who they're actually trying to reach. The result? Spray-and-pray campaigns, irrelevant outreach, and lists that go nowhere. 

Based on an analysis of 31 million outreach emails, Matt Tharp (CEO, Hunter) and Rui Costa (Product Manager, Hunter) reveal the exact framework to define your ideal customer profile (ICP), find your next best buyer, and build targeted lists that generate 158% more replies. 


What You'll Learn About Finding Your Target Audience: 
- Most B2B Lead Generation Fails Before It Starts: Discover why 61% of decision makers find cold email outreach completely irrelevant, and how poor targeting is always the root cause. 
- How to Define Your Ideal Customer Profile (ICP): Learn the difference between TAM, SAM, SOM, and your Prioritized Obtainable Market, and why most people build lists in the wrong ring entirely. 
- The Market → Company → Person Framework: A step-by-step framework to go from defining the space you want to target, all the way down to the individual decision maker with "hair on fire." 
- How to Use Hunter Discover to Validate Your ICP: Use filters for industry, headcount, revenue, location, hiring signals, and tech stack to build tightly-segmented lists of 100–200 people.
- Three Common ICP Mistakes That Kill Reply Rates: Contacting only one person per company, sending the same campaign to every contact, and failing to document who is NOT in your targeting. 
- The Data Behind Better Targeting: Lists under 100 recipients generate 158% more replies than lists of 500+. Contacting 2 people at one company improves reply rates by 46%. Emails with 2 custom attributes improve replies by 56%. 


Timestamps:
 00:00 - Welcome & Introductions
 03:30 - The Most Important Step in Lead Generation Most People Skip
 05:40 - The Spray-and-Pray Trap: What It Looks Like & What It Costs You
 08:00 - What Does the Data Tell Us? (31 Million Emails)
 11:30 - How to Think About Defining Your ICP (Not Assumptions)
 13:00 - Stop Chasing Everyone: Find Your Beachhead (TAM vs. POM)
 15:00 - The Market → Company → Person Framework
 19:00 - How to Use Hunter Discover to Find and Validate Your ICP
 22:00 - Three Common ICP Mistakes to Avoid
 22:30 - Mistake 1: Contacting Only One Person at a Company
 27:00 - Mistake 2: Sending One Campaign to Every Contact
 32:00 - Mistake 3: Failing to Document Who Is NOT Your Target
 38:00- The 6-Step Workflow: From Best Customers to Targeted Campaign
 42:00 - Pre-Campaign Checklist
 45:00 - Live Q&A: ICP, Hunter Discover, Exclusions & More 


📧 ICP & Target Audience FAQs Covered: 
✓ What is an ideal customer profile (ICP) and how do I define one? 
✓ What's the difference between TAM, SAM, SOM, and a Prioritized Obtainable Market? 
✓ Should I start from my existing customers or build a new ICP from scratch? 
✓ How do I know if a company has the will vs. the ability to buy? 
✓ How many people should be on a targeted outreach list? 
✓ Should I contact one person per company or multiple people? 
✓ What filters should I use in Hunter Discover to build a precise list? 
✓ How do I use hiring signals and funding data to spot “hair on fire” leads? 
✓ How do I build exclusion lists — and why does documenting your negative ICP matter? 
✓ What's the right number of custom attributes to include in an email? 
✓ How do I write a message that works for an entire segment? 
✓ When should I move on from a segment and build a new one? 

💡 Why This Matters: Most people who struggle with cold outreach are solving the wrong problem — they focus on subject lines, email copy, and send volume before they've answered the most fundamental question: who is this actually for? When your targeting is precise, your message writes itself. When it isn't, no amount of personalization or follow-up will save you. 

Data from 31 million outreach emails shows that list size alone (nothing else) can more than double your reply rate. That's not about copywriting. That's about targeting. 

This webinar is your step-by-step guide to getting that right first.

Your ICP becomes a Market Map in this lesson — defining your total, serviceable, and obtainable market, then ranking the firmographic and technographic segments where your best-fit customers actually cluster. It runs your ICP Statement and Scorecard from lesson four against the real market, since without that filter, segmentation is just picking industries you like. The prioritized segments you land on here are what the outreach playbook, two lessons from now, is built to reach.

Link above for the full printable workbook.

segments.text: Imagine you’re playing a game of darts, but you can’t see where the dartboard
is. You throw the dart and it lands about five feet away from the target.
Hope you didn’t bet any money on your skills this time.
Now change up that game. Let’s say you CAN see the board clearly, and instead of a complete miss,
you land on the board…maybe right near the center if you’re especially coordinated.
Knowing where the dart is supposed to go makes hitting your target a lot easier.
The point of that example is to illustrate the importance of knowing where to aim your B2B
marketing. If you don’t know who your target audience is and where they spend time online,
you’ll waste money and energy trying to reach the wrong people and businesses.
That’s where an ideal customer profile, or ICP, comes in. Keep watching to learn what an ICP is
and how you can use one! What is an ICP?
Let’s start by defining what an ICP is. Again, the term stands for “ideal customer profile,”
and it refers to a group of traits that define the businesses you want to reach with your products
or services. It’s sort of an outline of what the ideal business client looks like for your company.
Establishing what your ICP looks like allows you to steer your marketing in the right direction to
reach your best prospects. ICP vs. buyer persona
You might be thinking, “Hang on, this sounds familiar. Aren’t we just talking about buyer
personas?” And, while the two do sound similar, the answer is no — buyer personas and ICPs are two
different things. But they are connected. When you create a buyer persona, you’re
creating a fleshed-out, fictional, individual person. While your clients are businesses,
your buyer personas focus on specific decision-makers at those businesses. So,
one buyer persona might be “Sally, a 54-year-old marketing manager who works at a medium-sized
consulting firm. She’s concerned with X, Y, and Z, and is responsible for A,B, and C strategies.”
But with an ICP, you’re not focused on creating a fictionalized character that represents specific
people at certain companies — you’re focused on the companies themselves. You’re looking
at qualities like industry, size, and location. Maybe even the actions people
from that business take on your website. Basically, ICPs help you figure out which
businesses are your ideal clients, so you can target those businesses with your marketing.
Buyer personas, meanwhile, help you figure out which people at those companies will
see your marketing, what they need most from your business, and how you can optimize your
marketing so that it’s persuasive to them. You may be wondering how ICP marketing can
benefit you. Maybe you’re thinking, “I already know which kinds of businesses to market to!” And
maybe that’s true. You probably do have a good idea of which sorts of companies buy from you.
But here’s the thing — the more specific that knowledge is, the better. It’s one thing to know
that you should market to, let’s say, small pest control businesses in Kansas. But an
ICP can help you outline even more detailed info. Maybe your ideal clients aren’t just from Kansas,
but from a specific set of counties in northern Kansas. And maybe they’re not
just small businesses, but they’re specifically companies that have between 20 and 90 employees.
And those are just two examples — even if you already know both of those things, there
are plenty of other details your ICP can reveal. The result is that you can much more effectively
target your ideal audience — because you have a much more precise idea of who that audience is.

metadata.title: Ideal Customer Profile Template: Free B2B Worksheet & Examples
metadata.author: Misar AI
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode we walk you through a ready to copy Ideal Customer Profile worksheet, show two real B2B examples, and break down each section step by step. You'll learn how to fill out the template, why each question matters, and how to use the completed ICP to focus your sales and marketing efforts. From the article "Ideal Customer Profile Template: Free B2B Worksheet & Examples" by MisarReach, published on Misar.Blog.


Sponsored by: https://misarreach.com
In this episode:
0:00 Introduction
0:12 An Ideal Customer Profile (ICP) Describes the Companies Most Likely
0:50 Because an ICP Is a Filter for Accounts
1:20 The Worksheet Is Meant to Turn Each ICP Field into a Filter You Can Run
1:51 The Worksheet Includes Both Positive ICP Fields and Anti-ICP Disqualifiers
2:53 Worked Example 1 Shows a B2B SaaS ICP
4:04 That SaaS ICP Is Intended to Produce a Filtered Account List That Fits
4:50 Worked Example 2 Shows an Agency ICP
5:55 That Agency ICP Can Be Used to Prioritize Contacts with Intent Signals
6:34 An Anti-ICP Is Important Because It Tells You Which Accounts Waste Time


Topics: ideal customer profile, icp template, b2b worksheet, customer profiling, sales targeting, marketing strategy.


Questions this episode answers:
- Why is an anti-ICP important for B2B sales and marketing? An anti-ICP is important because it tells you which accounts waste time and budget.
- How often should an Ideal Customer Profile be reviewed? The ICP should be reviewed quarterly because market dynamics change.

Sending cold emails, but not getting the results you want? One of the reasons might be that you’re not sending your emails to the right people.

Watch this video to find out how to define your ideal customer profile to have a better chance at getting more replies and closing more deals.

To get the most results out of your outreach, you have to find the specific people that are most likely to want your product or service. That way you’ll:
- Increase reply and conversion rates
- Stop wasting money and time on people who are not your customers
- Perform better for your clients

In this video, we’ll walk you through 3 steps to determine your Ideal Customer Profile. 
An ICP is a hypothetical description of the type of company that would receive the most value from your product or solution.

Then, after you’ve determined your ICP, it’s important to remember that you’re actually going to sell your solution to people (not to the company itself). That’s why you need to identify the specific people within the company that you want to reach. We’ll show you how to establish your buyer persona and how to create a scrapable persona or one that you can use to find information about. 

Knowing all of this information about your clients will help you generate leads and close more deals.

metadata.title: Your Ideal Customer Profile (ICP): How It Changes Sales & Marketing
metadata.author: Prairie Founders Club
metadata.shortDescription:
Your Ideal Customer Profile (ICP) isn’t just a marketing exercise, it determines whether your business should be sales-led, marketing-led, or a blend of both.

In this lesson from Escape Corporate America: Revenue 101, we break down:

B2B vs B2C (and how it changes ticket size, decision-makers, and sales cycle length)

How to estimate Customer Lifetime Value (LTV) using a simple “total revenue ÷ total customers” approach

The quadrant that clarifies your operating model:

B2B + LTV over $10K → more sales-oriented

B2C + LTV under $10K → more marketing-oriented

The middle zones → you typically need both

How to define ICP deeper than demographics: pain points, awareness level (do they know they have the problem?), and the human traits that build trust

Key takeaway: you can’t build in a vacuum — businesses win by understanding people and solving real problems.

Subscribe for the rest of the Revenue 101 series, and if you want templates and community support, check out Prairie Founders Club.

#IdealCustomerProfile #ICP #SalesStrategy #MarketingStrategy #B2B #B2C #CustomerLifetimeValue #Entrepreneurship #PrairieFoundersClub

metadata.shortDescription:
Episode Overview:
AI is reshaping how businesses grow—and the winners are building with intention. In this episode of Marketing in the Age of AI, Emanuel Rose sits down with Jeff Borschowa to explore how AI, ICP precision, and “whale hunting” strategies are transforming marketing, sales, and business growth.
From the “agentic pivot” to building smarter systems, this conversation breaks down how to move beyond experimentation and start creating real, measurable value with AI.

What You’ll Learn:
- What the “agentic pivot” means for modern businesses
- Why ICP (Ideal Client Profile) precision beats mass targeting
- How “whale hunting” outperforms chasing small deals
- Using AI (Custom GPTs + systems) to operationalize growth
- The role of relationships vs transactions in AI-driven marketing
- How to prove ROI and avoid wasted effort in AI adoption

Featured Guest:
Jeff Borschowa is a strategist who helps B2B teams align sales, marketing, and operations to drive predictable revenue. Known for his systems-first approach, Jeff focuses on practical automation, ICP clarity, and measurable business impact—not hype.

Episode Highlights:
- The shift from “experimenting with AI” → “building with AI”
- Why most businesses waste energy targeting the wrong audience
- The Dream 100 concept reimagined as “AI whale hunting”
- How Jeff uses 400+ custom GPTs to model ICP behavior
- Leveraging conferences, networks, and ecosystems strategically
- Why adding value (not visibility) is the real growth lever
- The power of connection-driven marketing and long-term relationships

Connect and Explore More:
Connect with Emanuel Rose:
- LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/b2b-leadgeneration/
- Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/emanuelroseauthor/
- Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/EmanuelRoseAuthor
- YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/@marketingintheageofai-ec6fx
Connect with the Guest (Jeff Borschowa):
- LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/jeff-borschowa/

Further Reading or Resources:

https://emanuelrose.com/whale-hunting-with-ai-how-to-turn-icp-precision-into-revenue/
🌐 Learn more from Emanuel Rose:
https://emanuelrose.com/
📘 Get the book Authentic Marketing in the Age of AI:
https://emanuelrose.com/product/authentic-marketing-in-the-age-of-ai/


If you found value in this episode, make sure to like, subscribe, and comment with your biggest takeaway.
What’s your ICP strategy—and are you still chasing minnows or hunting whales?

metadata.shortDescription:
Most sales teams are still manually tracking enterprise accounts. By the time they find relevant news, competitors have already reached out.
This workflow changes that.
In this video, I walk through a complete signal-led outbound system I built for a client using Clay. It monitors 1,000+ enterprise accounts 24/7, filters signals with AI, enriches contacts automatically, and delivers everything to your team in Slack.
What you'll learn:

How to set up Clay Signals to track enterprise accounts automatically
Using AI (Claude) to filter noise and validate relevance
Building email + phone waterfalls for maximum coverage
Pushing enriched data to Slack and Google Sheets in real-time
Creating competitive advantage through GTM automation

Timestamps:
0:00 - Why signal-led outbound matters
0:42 - The client's problem: manual research at scale
2:14 - Setting up Clay Signals for account monitoring
3:30 - AI filtering with Claude to remove noise
5:00 - Automated contact enrichment (email + phone waterfalls)
7:12 - Pushing to Slack + Google Sheets in real-time
8:00 - The complete workflow recap

Tools mentioned:

Clay
Claude AI
Slack
Google Sheets

metadata.title: How To Build Signal Based Outreach Campaigns (Full Guide)
metadata.author: Hlib Storchak
metadata.shortDescription:
The best lead is the one who just did something. Signal-based outbound means you stop blasting static lists and start triggering your outreach off buying signals, something a prospect just did that means the pain is live right now. Same offer, a warmer person, far better timing, and reply rates jump from 2-3% to 15-25%.

I run outbound systems for B2B companies and we book 1,500+ sales calls a month for our clients. This is the exact shift that moved the needle most: targeting the signal instead of the title. In this video I break down what a buying signal actually is, the signals that pull the highest reply rates, four plays you can copy this week, and how to turn the whole thing into a system that feeds your pipeline on its own. Stick around for play 3, one filter change took a client from 0.8% to 11% replies with the same copy.

WHAT YOU WILL LEARN
• What a buying signal actually is, and why timing beats targeting beats copy
• The 7 signals that pull the highest reply rates in cold outreach
• Four signal-based plays you can copy this week
• How to catch signals without paying for expensive intent data
• How to write the opener so the signal is your first line
• How to turn signals into a system so your pipeline never goes cold

THE SIGNALS THAT ACTUALLY WORK
• New hire, they hired for the function you serve, the need is fresh
• Funding, they just raised, budget and pressure to grow
• Tech change, they added or dropped a tool you plug into
• Job change, a champion moved to a company that now needs you
• Website visit, they came to your site, the strongest intent there is
• Competitor engagement, they follow or engage with a competitor
• Content engagement, they liked or commented on a relevant post

THE FOUR PLAYS
1. Deanonymize your website visitors and reach out the same day, 15-25% replies vs 2-3% cold
2. Pull your competitor's followers, enrich and filter to the right title, then reach out, 18-25% replies
3. Swap a broad list for one hiring signal, "hired a Head of Data in the last 90 days", 0.8% to 11% replies
4. Clone your best customers, paste a best-customer domain into Prospeo, go straight at the lookalikes, 5-8% replies

WHO THIS IS FOR
B2B founders, sales leaders, SDR and BDR managers, RevOps, and agencies who want higher reply rates without buying pricey intent data.

CHAPTERS

1:10 Stop blasting lists, start catching signals

4:00 The signals worth chasing

WANT US TO BUILD THIS FOR YOU?

WHO I AM
I help B2B companies build outbound systems that actually work. We book 1,500+ sales calls per month for our clients using Clay, cold email, cold calling, and LinkedIn outbound. Subscribe for weekly videos on GTM strategy, cold email, Clay workflows, and B2B pipeline generation. New videos every week.

metadata.title: The Ultimate Signal-based Outbound Framework in 2026 (all in Clay)
metadata.author: Blue Pencil
metadata.shortDescription:
If I was hired to set up a signal-based outbound framework for a B2B tech company in MENA, this is the exact system I’d build — fully inside Clay.

In this video, I walk through a practical setup:

1) Build a Target Accounts table
Start with 200–500 accounts that match your ICP.

2) Track 3 tiers of signals inside Clay

Tier 1: Build signals (proof they’re investing)
Examples: hiring, promotions, integrations, new tech detected, initiative launches, headcount growth

Tier 2: Forcing functions (events that compress timelines)
Examples: funding, M&A, IPO, office expansion, major client wins

Tier 3: Confirmation signals (intent validation)
Attention (engagement/visits), Problem (posted/attended/mentioned pain), Ownership (role change/promotion)

3) Convert raw signals into 6 “reach out now” archetypes

Build + Attention

Force + Build

Problem + Build

New Leader Reset

Double Build

Multi-Actor Proof

4) Route messaging based on archetype
I show how to assign a message angle + CTA so outbound matches the moment (instead of generic sequences).

5) Run it as an ops loop
Weekly signal refresh → tag archetypes → only outreach when a tag fires → prioritize the highest-conviction plays first.

metadata.title: Build + launch outbound campaigns without leaving the terminal (Claude Code + Apollo)
metadata.author: ColdIQ
metadata.shortDescription:
One Unified API for all your GTM Data: https://coldiq.com/
Build your entire outbound campaign with Apollo: https://go.coldiq.com/apollo

In this live session, Mich (ColdIQ) and Brandon Reis (Apollo) build a complete outbound campaign end-to-end using the Apollo API and Claude Code, without ever leaving the terminal. No slides, no theory, just the build, live.

You'll see the full GTM engineering workflow: finding and building your ICP list, researching and enriching accounts in bulk, writing personalized copy with AI, then setting up and launching the campaign via API. 30 minutes of live build plus 15 minutes of Q&A.

Whether you're a founder, GTM engineer, SDR, or on a RevOps team, this session shows how to treat outbound like code, fast, repeatable, and fully in your control. Come with your ICP in mind and you'll leave with a campaign you can run the same day.

Connect with Mich on LinkedIn:   https://www.linkedin.com/in/michel-lieben/
Connect with Brandon on LinkedIn:   https://www.linkedin.com/in/brandonmreis/?utm_source=luma

metadata.title: Next-Level Outbound: Using Clay Signals & Apify for Real-Time Lead Gen
metadata.author: Josh Whitfield
metadata.shortDescription:
Tired of stale lead lists and slow GTM motions? This video is your insider look into how Clay’s Signals feature—when paired with tools like Apify—can dramatically transform your outbound strategy.

What you'll learn in this tutorial:

🔍 Advanced Signal Tracking: Discover how to go beyond built-in job changes and fundraising alerts by monitoring custom signals like post interactions, RSS feeds, and more.

🛠️ Real-Time API Automations: Learn how to connect any API in the world using Apify and Clay—scraping Hacker News job boards, monitoring keywords from Gong calls, and syncing insights directly to tools like Outreach, Instantly, or Hayreach.

⚙️ Workflow Orchestration with Clay: Set schedules, enrich leads, and automate campaigns as signals are triggered—no manual steps required.

💡 Creative Use Cases:

Scrape and track social interactions on your own LinkedIn posts

Monitor job boards and turn listings into enriched company records

Run automated lead flows into Salesforce, HubSpot, and beyond

Use simple API requests to unlock powerful, real-time signal streams

🚀 Why This Changes Everything:

metadata.title: Clay Masterclass for 2026: The GTM Workflows That Actually Move Pipeline (30+ Examples)
metadata.author: SalesCaptain
metadata.shortDescription:
In this session, Bill Stathopoulos (CEO, SalesCaptain) joins Frank Sondors (Salesforge) for a practical, no-fluff masterclass on the top Clay workflows to roll out into 2026.

This isn’t a Clay basics tutorial.
It’s a systems-level walkthrough of how modern GTM teams are using Clay as the data + orchestration layer to run AI outbound, intent-driven targeting, and inbound-led outbound at scale.

We cover:
– Why GTM got harder (saturation, higher CAC, slower payback) and what changed after late 2023
– The 3-bucket GTM model: AI Outbound, Intent Signals, Inbound-Led Outbound
– How Clay becomes the “warehouse” for company + people data (150+ integrations)
– Examples of workflows that replace repetitive BDR work (build once, scale forever)
– Personalization that actually feels human (without relying on LinkedIn posts)
– How to stack many small campaigns to compound pipeline (instead of betting on one big play)

If you lead sales, marketing, RevOps, or GTM and you’re trying to build a leaner team that produces more output in 2026, this is worth your time.

metadata.title: Trust and the Trojan Horse: Using Thought Leadership to Convince Internal Influencers
metadata.author: Joel Harrison B2B
metadata.shortDescription:
Trust and the Trojan Horse: Using Thought Leadership to Convince Internal Influencers with Annie Dunleavy of Edelman

Episode Description
In this episode of the 'Trust & Influence in B2B' podcast, host Joel Harrison speaks with Annie Dunleavy, EVP of Content Strategy at Edelman, about the critical role of internal influencers in B2B purchasing decisions. They explore Edelman's latest research revealing that over 40% of B2B deals stall due to internal misalignment, and how thought leadership can serve as a "Trojan horse" to reach hidden stakeholders who hold 50% of decision-making power but rarely interact with sales teams. Annie shares insights on why internal influencers prefer provocative content over validation, how quality thought leadership outperforms traditional marketing materials, and practical strategies for B2B marketers to engage these otherwise inaccessible audiences. Join them as they discuss the evolving complexity of B2B buyer groups and the future of thought leadership strategy.

Takeaways:
🎯 Hidden buyers hold 50% of decision-making power but are often overlooked by marketing efforts
📊 Internal influencers consume just as much thought leadership as formal decision makers (64% vs 63%)
🧠 86% of internal influencers want provocative ideas that challenge assumptions rather than validate existing thinking
🔓 95% say strong thought leadership makes them more receptive to future sales outreach
💪 71% view thought leadership as more effective than traditional marketing materials for demonstrating vendor capabilities
🤝 79% of internal influencers are more likely to champion RFP proposals from companies with strong thought leadership
🎨 60% of internal influencers prefer unique formats compared to 51% for target buyers
⚖️ 53% of both audiences agree that high-quality thought leadership matters more than brand recognition
📈 41% of decision makers have been encouraged by C-suite executives to consider vendors based on their thought leadership
🔄 Thought leadership creates internal virality, helping stakeholders advocate for vendors in closed-door conversations

Chapters:
01:32 - The Challenge of Internal Misalignment in B2B Deals 
02:39 - Understanding Hidden Buyers vs Target Buyers 
04:23 - Content Strategy for Internal Influencers 
06:10 - Why Internal Influencers Want Provocative Content 
08:58 - Thought Leadership as a Trojan Horse Strategy 
12:09 - Building Credibility vs Traditional Marketing Materials 
13:23 - Transforming Skeptics into Internal Advocates 
15:10 - Creating Human-Accessible Content Formats 
18:01 - Levelling the Playing Field for Challenger Brands 
19:08 - C-Suite Influence and Top-Down Momentum 
20:17 - Measuring Impact on Internal Influencers 
25:28 - Three Key Recommendations for B2B Marketers 
27:59 - The Future of Internal Influences and Buyer Complexity

Resources Mentioned:
🔎 The Jolt Effect by Matt Dixon - amazon.com/Jolt-Effect-Hard-Customers-Decide/dp/059308076X 
🔎 LinkedIn and Bain Research on Buying Committees - business.linkedin.com   
🔎 Edelman's 2025 B2B Thought Leadership Report - edelman.com 

Follow Annie Dunleavy:
https://linkedin.com/in/anniedunleavy/
Edelman - https://edelman.com

Follow Joel Harrison:
https://linkedin.com/in/joelharrison/

🔔 Subscribe to the channel for weekly insights, interviews, and on-the-ground perspectives from
the world of B2B marketing.
https://youtube.com/@JoelHarrison-B2B?sub_confirmation=1

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Welcome to the official YouTube channel of Joel Harrison B2B.
This is your inside track to the ever-evolving world of business-to-business marketing—told
through the lens of someone who’s lived and breathed it for over two decades. I’m Joel Harrison,
founder of B2B Marketing, creator of Propolis, and host of the Trust & Influence in B2B Marketing
podcast. Through this channel, I bring you real conversations with the people driving change,
navigating complexity, and building the next generation of marketing leadership.
➡ Expect regular videos filmed on the move—from major events like Ignite, to behind-the-scenes
interviews, to deeper dives into topics that matter most to today’s marketers. We’ll explore what
it means to be a commercial marketer, how to build trust and credibility in technical sectors, and
how thought leadership can evolve beyond buzzwords into something truly impactful. You’ll hear
from voices at the cutting edge of B2B, including marketers from global brands, fast-growing
startups, and everything in between.
This isn’t theory for theory’s sake. It’s about helping you become more effective, influential, and
commercially grounded—so you can thrive in a fast-moving, high-expectation world.

metadata.title: The Trojan Horse Sales Strategy with Brian Gilman
metadata.author: Winston Francois
metadata.shortDescription:
Episode #245: Brian Gilman - Why the funnel breaks when you sell to the C-suite

Why meetings, not MQLs, are the number that predicts pipeline on six- and seven-figure deals.

For B2B marketers selling mission-critical products to chief risk and compliance officers in regulated industries.

Brian Gilman is the CMO of ThetaRay, which sells cognitive AI that helps banks and fintechs catch financial crime. His buyers are skeptical, the incumbents are entrenched, and many banks still treat AI as a risk. Brian explains why he organizes marketing by region instead of funnel stage, how ThetaRay sells an agentic AI layer that sits on top of existing rules-based systems instead of asking banks to rip and replace, and how a company with 13 years of machine learning history stands out when every competitor claims AI. He also shares the math he reports to his board: for every 10 meetings, he gets a predictable number of opportunities.

WHAT YOU'LL HEAR
- Why the traditional MQL funnel fails with C-suite buyers, and why meetings are the metric Brian reports to his executive team and board
- How ThetaRay's financial crime experts flag new regulations, like the Central Bank of Nigeria's AML upgrade requirement, so marketing can launch social and ABM campaigns fast
- Why AI buzzwords make credible companies sound like everyone else, and why prospects often try to build in-house before coming back
- How to rethink the marketing mix toward partners, events, and curated dinners where $5,000 gets twenty buyers in a room

CHAPTERS / TIMESTAMPS
00:00 - Why the funnel breaks for big-ticket sales
02:03 - What's broken in anti-money laundering today
02:51 - Why $260 billion in AML software hasn't forced banks to switch
03:51 - Sitting on top of incumbents instead of replacing them
05:09 - Selling to banks vs. fintechs
06:32 - Product marketing by persona
07:46 - Organizing marketing by region, not funnel stage
08:36 - Why meetings beat MQLs with the C-suite
11:03 - Building campaigns around regulatory events
11:52 - Standing out when everyone claims AI
13:47 - Competing against build
14:51 - Selling AI to buyers who fear it
15:52 - Rethinking the marketing mix: partners, events and dinners
17:15 - Lightning round
17:57 - Top three takeaways and one action for this week

LINKS & RESOURCES
Guest
- Brian Gilman - CMO, ThetaRay
- https://www.thetaray.com
- https://www.linkedin.com/in/bgilman1/

ABOUT FRANK GROWTH
Frank Growth is a podcast about how companies actually grow - real operators, real constraints, real decisions. Hosted by Jason Shafton.

PROMOTIONAL LINKS
- Work with Winston Francois: https://wf.team/podcast
- Subscribe / Follow Jason: https://www.linkedin.com/in/jasonshafton/

metadata.title: How Gal Ko and PodStar Turn Podcast Guesting Into B2B Growth
metadata.author: AI InterConnect
metadata.shortDescription:
Gal Ko shares insights on how B2B technology funders can leverage podcast appearances to build authority, generate business opportunities, and create a content flywheel that accelerates growth.

 key  topics
Podcast guesting as a strategic tool for B2B funders
The PodStar model for positioning and relationship building
How to select the right podcasts for maximum impact
Repurposing podcast content for broader reach
Using podcasts to shorten sales cycles in complex B2B sales
Building a community around podcast appearances
The importance of authenticity and storytelling in podcasts
AI tools for identifying valuable podcast opportunities

 takeaways
Podcast appearances should focus on sharing value and building relationships, not direct selling.
Selecting the right podcasts involves assessing size, signal, topic fit, activity, and engagement.
A small, niche podcast can sometimes create more value than a large, broad one.
Repurposing podcast content across channels amplifies reach and authority.
Post-appearance content sharing and strategic networking turn podcasts into business opportunities.
Systematic outreach and automation can scale podcast guesting efforts.
Authenticity and storytelling are key to resonating with podcast audiences.
AI tools can help identify and vet the best podcasts for your target audience.
Building a community around podcasting efforts creates long-term value.
Consistency and systemization are crucial for scaling podcast-based authority building.

"Niche podcasts can create more targeted value than broad shows."
"Use past guests to identify strategic partners and buyers."

In this video, I’ll break down each of the different HubSpot Lifecycle Stages, including, Subscriber, Lead, MQL, SQL, Opportunity and Customer. I'll tell you how each stage is typically defined and how they each fit together in the overall marketing funnel:

0:32 - Subscriber: Newsletter and low-intent lead forms

1:50 - Sales Qualified Lead (SQL): Sales call and validation 
2:34 - Opportunity: The first stage with associated deal value 
3:20 - Customer: Closed-won deals and attribution considerations 
3:38 - Warning: Avoiding false customer conversions in ad platforms 
4:38 - Summary and how these stages impact conversion tracking

metadata.title: HubSpot CRM Tutorial for Beginners (2026) – Full Free Setup
metadata.author: Biz Stack School
metadata.shortDescription:
Set up HubSpot's free CRM from an empty account to a working sales system, one step at a time. We build it for a real-looking business, Tallgrass & Tin Roofing in Austin, Texas, so every contact, deal and report you see is something you can copy for your own company.

👉 Try HubSpot CRM free: https://bizstackschool.web.app/hubspot/9qyxufkz05c

By the end you'll have contacts imported, companies linked, a custom sales pipeline with 20 deals, products with prices, tasks and logged calls, email templates, saved views and your first dashboard. All on the free plan, no credit card, no paid trial.

⏱ Chapters
0:00 What you'll build
0:32 Step 1 – Pick the free HubSpot plan
2:34 Step 2 – Your first five minutes in HubSpot
4:52 Step 3 – Import contacts from a CSV
8:24 Step 4 – Companies and associations
11:08 Step 5 – Custom properties
13:55 Step 6 – Build your sales pipeline and import deals
19:45 Step 7 – Add products and prices
22:53 Step 8 – Tasks, calls and activities
26:15 Step 9 – Email templates
29:34 Step 10 – Saved views and filters
32:31 Step 11 – Your first dashboard
35:25 What you built and next steps

📌 Good to know
