segments.text: By the end of this video, this is yours. A working customer relationship manager, built from an empty account.
You can see it behind me. A pipeline full of jobs, sixty contacts, six companies, and a dashboard that tells you where the money is.
We are going to build every piece of it together, one step at a time.
The company is a roofing business in Austin, Texas, called Tallgrass and Tin Roofing.
It is fictional, but the problems are real. Let's start with step one.
Step one of twelve. Pick the free plan.
Before we build anything, you need an account. Open the HubSpot website, and go to the pricing page.
You will see several products, each with a few tiers.
Do not worry about most of it.
For this whole video, we need one thing, and it costs nothing.
Look at the first column, Free. Zero dollars. That free customer relationship manager is what we use today.
Next to it is a paid tier called Starter. It is a fine choice later, if your business grows into it.
But you do not need it to follow along.
The free plan gives you the core. You can store contacts and companies, track deals, log calls, and see basic reports.
The paid plans add automation, more advanced reporting, and extra seats and limits.
They are not where you begin.
So click the button that says get started free. HubSpot will ask for your email address.
Use a real one that you can open, because you will need to confirm it.
You can sign up with a Google account if you prefer. Next, it will ask for your name, your company name, and a few questions about your business.
Type in Tallgrass and Tin Roofing. For company size, pick two to five.
We are a small crew. Next, you may see screens to connect your email, or to set things up with A I.
Skip those for now. Choose the options that keep you on the free plan.
We are not starting any trials in this video. When the setup finishes, you will land on your home screen.
It will look mostly empty. That is exactly what we want.
A blank account is a clean place to build good habits. One last tip before we move on.
Your account also has a time zone and a currency. You will find both in settings, behind the gear.
Our company is in Austin, so in your own account, pick central time and United States dollars.
Setting this now saves confusing numbers later. Good.
You have an account. Let's find our way around.
Step two of twelve. Your first five minutes.
A new account can feel crowded, so let's slow down and look at what matters.
Start on the left side of the screen. That column is the main menu.
Click through the first few items. Contacts, companies, deals, and tasks. Further down, you will see dashboards.
Do not click into every tool. Most of them are not for you today.
Here is the big idea of this whole system. A customer relationship manager is built on four kinds of records.
HubSpot calls them objects. There are four you need to know.
The first is contacts. A contact is a person.
A homeowner who calls about a leak is a contact. The second is companies.
A company is an organization. A vet clinic, or a homeowners association, is a company.
The third is deals. A deal is a chance to earn money.
It is a specific job, with a price and an expected date.
A gutter replacement for eighteen hundred dollars could be a deal. Our board is still empty. The fourth is tickets.
A ticket is a support request, something a customer needs help with after the sale.
We will not use tickets in this video. Many small businesses never do.
So the picture is simple. People work at companies.
People and companies have deals. That is nearly all you need to understand.
Now let's talk about what to ignore. Under more, you will see marketing, service, automation, and many other tools.
These are useful for bigger teams. For now, leave them alone.
Learning fewer things well beats learning many things badly. Back to the contacts page.
HubSpot adds two sample contacts, and that is fine. Notice the table layout, the search bar, and the button to add contacts.
This table view is where you will spend most of your time.
Open the deals page. You will see a board with columns.
We will shape it to fit our business in a later step.
Last, notice the settings icon, the little gear in the top bar.
Settings is where you control properties, pipelines, and users. We will visit it several times.
That is your map. Four objects, one table, one gear.
Let's put some people in it.
Step three of twelve. Import your contacts.
Typing sixty people by hand would take a long time, so we will import them from a spreadsheet instead.
In the description, you will find a file called contacts dot c s v.
Download it and open it in any spreadsheet app. Take a look before we upload it.
This habit saves a lot of trouble. The first row holds the column names.
First name, last name, email, phone number, company name, job title, city, state, lifecycle stage, and lead source.
Each row after that is one person. Check that your data is clean.
Are the names spelled consistently? Is every email address in its own column?
Do the rows look like a simple table with no merged cells?
A clean file imports smoothly. A messy file creates messy records.
Now go back to HubSpot. On the empty contacts page, click import data from a file.
HubSpot asks how you would like to start. Choose quick import, which brings in contacts from one file.
Upload the file. HubSpot will read it and show you a mapping screen.
This is the most important part of the import, so let's go through it carefully.
Mapping means telling HubSpot which column in your file matches which property in the system.
HubSpot is good at guessing. Where the column name matches, it will connect them for you.
First name goes to first name. Email goes to email.
Look at every row in the mapping list. If a column is marked as unmapped, decide what to do.
Most of ours will match. Lead source does not exist yet, so open the drop down, and create a new property for it.
Now here is a key idea. Email is the unique key.
HubSpot uses the email address to recognize a person. If you import someone whose email already exists, HubSpot updates the existing record.
It does not make a second copy. This is how you avoid duplicates.
It is also a reason to always include an email address. A contact without one is harder to protect from doubles.
Pay attention to two columns in particular. Lifecycle stage tells you where a person is in your relationship.
Some of ours are leads, and some are customers. Lead source tells you how they found us, such as Facebook, a Google search, or a repeat visit.
Both will be useful in our reports later. Name your import, Tallgrass contacts, and pick a legal basis, such as legitimate interest, customer.
Before that, HubSpot scanned the file. Zero errors, in sixty rows.
We expect sixty. Click finish, and wait a moment.
When the import is done, open the contacts page. There they are.
Sixty people, with names, emails, phone numbers, and cities.
Each one has its own record, with details, a timeline, and linked records.
This list is the starting point for everything that follows.
We will fill in those parts in the next steps. Here is a quick test of the duplicate protection.
Imagine you import the same file a second time. Nothing doubles.
HubSpot matches each email and updates what is already there. That is the safety net, and it is worth trusting but also checking, so always glance at the count.
One more habit to build. Whenever you import, keep the original file.
If something looks wrong later, you can compare the record against your source.
Your people are in. Next, we connect them to their companies.
Step four of twelve. Companies and associations.
A person is only part of the story. Many of our customers are businesses, and we want to see all the people and all the jobs for each one.
Open the companies page. You may already see a few companies here.
That is because HubSpot creates a company from the email domain of your contacts, when it recognizes a business address.
Tallgrass works with six companies. They include a vet clinic in Round Rock, a homeowners association in Cedar Park, and a few others.
Some of them are already here, created from those email domains.
To add the rest, and the city for each one, we use an import, just as we did with contacts.
Click add companies, then import. Choose advanced imports, select companies, upload companies dot c s v, and check the mapping.
Finish the import. Now every company is in the list, with its city.
Now for the most important word in this chapter. Associations.
An association is a link between two records. It says this person belongs to that company.
Or this deal is for that contact. Open the company Pecan Street Bakery, then its contact, Linda Alvarez.
Her email address ends with the bakery's domain. Look at the right side of her record.
You will see a section for companies. HubSpot links a contact to a company automatically, when the email domain matches.
Check whether that has happened. If it has, you will see the bakery listed there.
If it has not, click add on the companies card, search for the company, and select it.
The link appears on both sides. On the bakery's record, Linda is listed as a contact, next to her colleagues.
That is the whole mechanism. Why does this matter?
Because associations let you see the full picture. Open a company, and every person, deal, call, and email sits in one place.
You do not have to search through three lists.
You can also set a primary company for a contact, which helps when a person is connected to more than one organization.
Most of our contacts are homeowners, so they have no company at all.
That is perfectly normal. Do not force a link where none exists.
Take a minute and connect the rest of the business contacts to their companies.
Work through them one at a time. It is a small job, and it pays off in every report you build later.
When you finish, open the companies list. You should see our six companies.
Each name appears once, with its city and phone number. A clean list is a good sign.
Your records now know who belongs where. Next, we add something custom.
Step five of twelve. Custom properties.
Every record in HubSpot is made of properties. A property is simply a field.
First name is a property. Phone number is a property.
City is a property. HubSpot gives you plenty of ready made fields.
But your business has its own details. A roofing company cares about something that a software company never would.
The type of roof. So let's create a property called roof type.
Click the gear icon to open settings. In the left menu, find properties.
The properties page opens on contact properties. That is what we want, because a roof type belongs to a person who owns a house.
Click create property. You will be asked for a few things.
Type the label, roof type. HubSpot will write a name behind the scenes for you.
HubSpot puts every field into a group, to keep related fields together.
Our field lands in contact information. You can see it in the table.
Now choose the field type. This is where you decide how people will fill it in.
For roof type, we want a drop down. A free text box would let people type shingle, Shingle, shingles, and asphalt shingle.
Four spellings for one thing. That ruins your reports.
A drop down keeps it clean. Add the options.
Asphalt shingle. Metal.
Tile. And flat, or T P O.
Four options are enough. Keep the list short.
You can always add more. Click create.
That is the entire job. The property exists.
Now let's see where it shows up. Open a contact record, for example Ashley Alvarez.
Look at the left side, in the section called key information.
The new field is not there yet. Open the actions menu, choose edit card properties, search for roof, tick roof type, and save.
Now choose a value. Set Ashley to asphalt shingle.
There is no save button here. The value is stored on her record right away.
From now on, roof type appears in this section on every contact record.
Keep it near the top, so your team sees it first. That small change helps people actually use the field.
You can also use this property in filters and lists. Later, we can ask for every customer with a metal roof, or every lead with a tile roof.
That is the power of a custom property. It turns a detail in your head into a column you can sort.
A word of caution. Do not create a property for everything.
Every new field is one more thing for your team to fill in.
Ask yourself before you add one. Will we use this in a report, a filter, or a decision?
If the answer is no, skip it. Next, the heart of the system.
The pipeline.
Step six of twelve. Build your pipeline.
This is the biggest step, so settle in. A pipeline is the path a deal takes from first contact to a final answer.
Yes or no. Won or lost.
Every business has its own path. A software company moves through demos and trials.
A roofing company moves through inspections and quotes. HubSpot gives you a generic set of stages, and our job is to rename them to match reality.
Open the deals page. Click the menu with the pipeline name, sales pipeline, and choose manage pipelines.
You will see five standard stages. Appointment scheduled, qualified to buy, presentation scheduled, decision maker bought in, and contract sent.
Those names are built for a different kind of company. Let's think about how a roof job really goes.
Someone calls. We book an inspection.
We climb up, look around, and then we send a quote. If they accept it, we schedule the work.
And in the end, the job is either won or lost. So our stages are these.
Inspection booked. Inspection done.
Quote sent. Quote accepted. Job scheduled.
Closed won. And closed lost.
Click on the first stage and rename it to inspection booked. Then rename the second to inspection done.
The third becomes quote sent, the fourth becomes quote accepted, and the fifth becomes job scheduled.
Below them, HubSpot always keeps two special closing stages, one for won and one for lost.
They are important, because reports use them to decide what counts as revenue.
Leave them as closed won and closed lost. Next to each stage, you will see a probability.
This is HubSpot's guess at how likely a deal is to close.
Early stages get a low number. Later stages get a higher number.
Adjust them to match what you really see. We keep the defaults for now, and that is fine.
You do not need to be perfect. Start with honest guesses, and tune them after a few months of real results.
Save your changes. Go to the deals page, and look at the board.
Your columns now speak the language of your business. Anyone on the team can read it at a glance.
Now let's fill it. We have twenty deals in a C S V file.
Here are its columns, as HubSpot reads them. Deal name, amount, deal stage, close date, contact email, and pipeline.
Notice the deal stage column. The words in your file must match your stage names exactly.
If the file says quote sent, and your stage says quote sent, they will match.
If the file says quoted, they will not. This is the number one reason deal imports fail.
Our file was prepared to match the new stage names, so we are ready.
Go to the deals page, open the add deals menu, and choose import. Click import data, then pick advanced imports.
Tick two objects, contacts and deals, because one file will create the deals and link them to people who already exist.
For contacts, choose to update existing records only, so the import never creates a duplicate person. Then upload the file.
On the mapping screen, check each column. Deal name, amount, deal stage, close date, and pipeline go to deal properties.
If a column lands in the wrong place, open its import as menu, and pick deal properties.
The contact email column goes to the contact. That is what links each deal to its person.
Check every row of the mapping, including pipeline. In an advanced import, HubSpot needs to know which pipeline every deal belongs to.
We will check the result at the end, because imports with links are a place where small things go wrong.
Name the import Tallgrass deals, choose the legal basis for the contacts, and finish the import.
Review the summary. Twenty deals created, twenty associations, and zero errors.
That is a clean import. Open the board.
You should now see cards spread across the columns. Each card shows the deal name, the amount, and the close date.
Let's look at a few. A roof inspection for one hundred ninety nine dollars, already won.
A gutter replacement for eighteen hundred dollars, won in October. A shingle repair for six hundred fifty dollars, waiting after inspection.
Click one card. You will see the deal record, much like a contact.
The preview shows the amount, the close date, the pipeline, and the stage. We will open the full record in a moment.
As each job moves forward, your team moves its card to the next column.
The stage updates. That simple motion is how your team will use the pipeline every day.
Someone finishes an inspection, and the card moves on. At the bottom of each column, HubSpot adds up the value of the deals in it.
This is a first look at your money. You can already see how much is waiting at the quote stage, which is often where a business loses track of things.
A few cleanup tips. If your deals look wrong after the import, do not panic.
On the import summary, you can clean up your import, fix your file, and run it again.
This is another reason to keep your original files. Also think about who owns each deal.
Every deal has an owner, the person responsible for it. Ours show no owner yet. When you import, you can map an owner column.
On a small team, ownership keeps jobs from falling through the cracks.
Take a breath. This was the longest step, and it was the most important one.
You now have a real pipeline, full of real looking jobs. Next, we tell HubSpot what we sell.
Step seven of twelve. Products.
Right now, our deals have an amount, but they do not say what was sold.
Products fix that. A product is something you sell, saved once, with a name and a price.
When you add it to a deal, you do not retype anything.
You pick it from a list. Tallgrass sells five services.
A roof inspection, for one hundred ninety nine dollars. A shingle repair covering up to one hundred square feet, for six hundred fifty dollars.
A gutter replacement, for eighteen hundred dollars. A storm damage repair, for four thousand two hundred dollars.
And a full roof replacement, for fourteen thousand five hundred dollars. Open the more menu, then C R M, then products.
This is your products library. It is empty for now.
Open the add products menu, and choose create a product. Let's make the first one by hand, so you see every field.
Name it roof inspection, set the type to service, and the unit price to one hundred ninety nine.
For the description, write full roof inspection with photo report. Then click create.
For the other four, use an import. Our file has a name, a unit price, and a description for each service.
Open add products, choose import, then advanced imports, and products. Upload the file, check the mapping, and name the import Tallgrass services.
Finish it. Four new products join the roof inspection.
Now all five services are in the library. Check the prices carefully.
A typo in a price will follow you into every deal. Now let's use them.
Open a deal, the shingle repair for Ashley Alvarez. At first, the record has no line items section.
Click customize, add the line items card to the default view, and save. Now the section is there.
On the line items card, click add, then select from product library, and pick shingle repair. HubSpot fills in the name and the price, six hundred fifty dollars.
You can change the quantity, or add a discount. Keep the quantity at one, and save.
The deal amount still says manual, six hundred fifty dollars. It matches the line item, and that is what counts.
That means the number on the card matches what you actually plan to charge.
You are no longer guessing. Why does this help?
Because later you can ask a better question. Which service brings in the most money?
Which one do we sell the most often? A simple list of deals cannot answer that.
Products can. There is also a lesson here about keeping data honest.
If everyone types an amount by hand, you will see slightly different numbers for the same job.
If everyone picks a product, the numbers agree. Try adding line items to two or three more deals.
Do not feel you must update all twenty right now. Start with the ones that matter, and use products from here on, for every new deal.
Your catalog is ready. Now, let's talk about keeping in touch.
Step eight of twelve. Tasks and activities.
A pipeline shows you where deals are. Activities show you what to do next.
This is the part that actually makes you money. Let's start with the simplest activity, logging a call.
Open a deal. Let's use the shingle repair for Ashley Alvarez, who is waiting on a quote.
On the record, click the activities tab, in the middle of the page.
You will see tabs like notes, emails, calls, tasks, and meetings. Open calls, and click log a call.
Why log a call, and not call? Placing calls from HubSpot is a paid feature, as that popup showed. Logging a call you made from your phone is free.
A box opens. Pick the contact, Ashley, then set the outcome to connected, and the direction to outbound.
Write a short note. Called Ashley after the inspection. Two shingles missing on the north side. She wants a quote for the repair this week.
Under the note, tick the box to create a follow up task. The default, in three business days, is fine. Then log the activity.
Your call is now part of the story, in order. Anyone on your team who opens this record can read it, so no more asking in the group chat what happened last Tuesday.
When something matters, write it down in the record, not in your head, and not on a sticky note.
Now, a task. A task is a reminder with a due date.
Click the task button at the top of the deal. Title it, send quote to Ashley Alvarez.
The due date is in two business days, at eight in the morning. That works.
Add a reminder one hour before, and set the priority to high.
Click create. The task is now attached to the deal.
It also shows on your own task list. Open the tasks page from the main menu. If an upgrade offer pops up, close it.
You will see all tasks, with quick views for due today, overdue, and upcoming. Here are our two tasks.
This page can become your daily to do list. Each morning, open it and start at the top.
Here is a good habit. Whenever you finish an activity, ask yourself, what happens next?
Then create the next task before you close the record. A deal without a next step is a deal that quietly dies.
Tasks work the same way from a contact or a company record.
Wherever you create one, it lands on the same task list, so nothing gets lost.
Meetings are another type of activity. If you book site visits, you can log them under the meetings tab.
You can also connect your email and calendar. We skip it here. It saves typing, but it shares data, so read each permission first.
The reminder we set will notify you before the task is due.
You can fine tune these alerts later, in your notification settings. Do not turn everything on.
Too many alerts and you will ignore them all. Choose the ones that help you act.
Finally, notice that every activity is stored on the record. Over time, you build a full history of each customer.
When someone calls after two years, you can see what you quoted, what they chose, and what you promised.
That history is the real value of a customer relationship manager. It is memory, shared by everyone.
Next, let's save you from retyping emails.
Step nine of twelve. Email templates.
You will send some version of the same message again and again.
A quote, a follow up, a thank you. Templates save you from writing them from scratch every time.
First, find the templates area. Click the search bar at the top, find in HubSpot, and type templates.
Open message templates, and click start from scratch. First, give it a name, your roof quote.
Then the subject line. Keep it clear and plain.
For example, your roof quote from Tallgrass and Tin Roofing. Now the body.
Write it the way you would speak to a neighbor. Start with a greeting.
Type hi, and a space. Now comes the first thing to learn about templates.
They can pull in details from the record. These are called personalization tokens.
Click insert, then personalization tokens. Pick contact, search for first name, and add it. When the email goes out, HubSpot replaces it with the real name.
Write the next line. Thanks for having us out to look at your roof. Here is your quote.
Then one line per service. Shingle repair, up to one hundred square feet, six hundred fifty dollars.
Then the next step. Reply to this email or call us, and we will get you on the schedule.
Add a clear closing, with the company name. Tallgrass and Tin Roofing.
Keep the whole message short. People read short emails.
Now, a few cautions. Always set a fallback for each token.
If a contact has no first name saved, the fallback steps in. Set it to the word there.
If the name is missing, the email reads, hi there, and not hi blank. This small detail prevents embarrassing mistakes.
Preview the template with a real contact. Pick Ashley Alvarez, click generate, and check that her name appears.
Read it out loud. If it sounds stiff, loosen it.
Now save the template. Its name, your roof quote, says exactly what it is.
A clear name helps you find it later. On the free plan, you can keep up to three templates, and the counter shows one of three created.
To send it, you need an inbox connected to HubSpot. We skip that in this demo account. In yours, open a contact, click email, choose the template, and add one personal line about their roof.
That is the best of both worlds. Fast, and still human.
We are using fake addresses in this video, so nothing real will go out.
In your own account, you will send to real people. Always double check the recipient before you press send.
Think about a few more templates to create over time. A follow up after three days.
A thank you after the job. A reminder before an inspection.
Build them as the need appears, not all at once. One more thing worth knowing.
When you send an email through HubSpot, it logs on the contact timeline automatically, if your email is connected.
You will see when it was sent, and in many cases when it was opened.
Use that information as a hint, not as proof. An open does not always mean the person read it.
Your messages are ready. Now let's make it easy to find the right people.
Step ten of twelve. Views and filters.
By now, you have a lot of data. Sixty contacts, twenty deals, six companies.
Imagine that growing to six hundred, or six thousand. You need a way to see just the slice you care about.
That is what filters do. And when you save a filter, it becomes a view.
Go to the contacts page. Next to the view tabs, click the plus, and choose create new view.
Pick the table layout, and name it customers in Austin.
Now open advanced filters. Add a filter, choose city, and pick Austin. Eleven contacts match.
Add a second filter. Choose lifecycle stage, and pick customer.
Now the table shows only customers in Austin. In our data, that is two people.
Both conditions must be true. Look at the count below the table.
It tells you how many records match. If it feels wrong, check your filters.
A common mistake is spelling a city differently from the data. Now save it.
Click save. HubSpot confirms the view was updated.
Its name, customers in Austin, stays on the tab.
It now appears as a tab above the table. Anyone on your team can click it and see the same list, without rebuilding it.
Let's make a second view, this time for deals. Go to the deals page, click the plus next to the tabs, and choose a table.
Name it open quotes. Add a filter for the deal stage, and pick two stages, quote sent and quote accepted.
Seven deals match. Save it. This one is powerful, because quotes are where follow up matters most.
Each Monday, open the view, and call everyone on the list. You can also choose which columns the table shows.
Use the option to edit columns, and add the amount and the close date if they are missing.
Remove the ones you never look at. A tidy table is easier to scan.
You can sort the table too. Click a column header to order by amount, from largest to smallest.
This lets you see your biggest opportunities first. Filters can use property values, like our roof type.
For example, you could filter your contacts by roof type, metal.
You get a list of everyone with a metal roof. If you ran a promotion for metal roofs, that is your audience.
A note on limits. The free plan may restrict how many saved views you can keep.
If you reach a limit, keep the views you use every week, and delete the rest.
Fewer, better views beat a long list nobody opens. Also consider lists.
A list is a saved group of contacts that you can use for emails or reports.
A view is how you look at records. A list is a group you can act on.
For our purposes today, views are enough. You can now find any customer in seconds.
Time to see the whole business at once.
Step eleven of twelve. Your first dashboard.
Everything we have done so far has been about recording data. Now we turn it into answers.
Here is the dashboards page. HubSpot already has a default dashboard, called C R M data overview.
You can use it, or create your own. Let's create one.
Click create dashboard, choose a new dashboard, and name it Tallgrass sales. Next, add reports.
The add reports panel opens by itself. HubSpot has many ready made reports.
On the free plan, you will have access to a good set of them.
Some may be locked behind paid plans, and that is fine. We need only a few.
Search for pipeline. The first report to add is deals by stage.
It shows how many deals sit at each stage of our pipeline.
Add it to the dashboard. You will see a chart, with a slice for each stage.
This answers a key question. Where are our jobs right now?
The second report is deals by status. It splits your deals into open and won.
In our data, it shows four open and two won, this quarter so far.
With both added, you have two views side by side.
What we might win, and what we have won. Let's look at what the charts tell us.
In our data, one job is booked for inspection, two are inspected, and one quote is out.
Six quotes are accepted, five jobs are scheduled, and five are already won. The story is easy to read, because the stages are in our own language.
Later, you can add a third report. Something about new contacts by lead source.
It shows where your customers come from, whether Facebook, Google, or word of mouth.
If one source brings the best jobs, spend more time there. You can also arrange the dashboard.
Drag the reports into a layout you like. Put the most important at the top left, because that is where your eyes go first.
Resize them so the numbers are easy to read. Check the filters at the top of the dashboard.
You can set a date range, such as this quarter. You can also filter by owner, to see one person at a time.
A word on trust. A dashboard is only as good as the data behind it.
If people forget to update stages, the charts will lie. That is why we built simple habits.
Drag the card. Log the call.
Create the next task. Share the dashboard if you want.
You can make it visible to your team, so that everyone sees the same numbers.
A weekly look at this page can replace a long status meeting.
Here is a routine to try. Every Monday, open the dashboard.
Check the pipeline. Then open your open quotes view.
Work through your tasks. That ten minute routine is the whole system in action.
And that is it. You have built a working customer relationship manager.
That brings us to the end. In about forty minutes, we went from an empty account to a business ready to run.
Let's look back at what you built. You picked the free plan, and found your way around.
You imported sixty contacts, with email as the key that keeps duplicates out.
You added six companies, and linked the people to them. You created a custom property for roof type.
You built a pipeline that speaks your language, and filled it with twenty deals.
You added your products, logged calls, and set tasks. You wrote an email template, saved two views, and built your first dashboard.
That is a real system. And you built it step by step, without paying for anything.
Now, one honest note. HubSpot changes its screens often.
The buttons in your account may sit in a slightly different place.
If so, look for the same words, and you will find your way.
The ideas stay the same, even when the menus move. What should you do next?
Use it. Put in your own contacts, and your own deals.
Rename the stages to match how you really work. Do it this week, while the steps are fresh.
In the next video, we go deeper into HubSpot for sales.
We will look at how to manage your daily work, follow up with more discipline, and turn more quotes into jobs.
The link will be in the description. All the sample files from this video are there too, so you can follow along with the same data.
If this helped, a like helps others find it. And if you have a question, leave it in the comments.

I will see you in the next one.

This is HubSpot's guess at how likely a deal is to close. Early stages get a low number. Later stages get a higher number. Adjust them to match what you really see. We keep the defaults for now, and that is fine. You do not need to be perfect. Start with honest guesses, and tune them after a few months of real results. Save your changes. Go to the deals page, and look at the board. Your columns now speak the language of your business. Anyone on the team can read it at a glance. Now let's fill it. We have twenty deals in a C S V file. Here are its columns, as HubSpot reads them. Deal name, amount, deal stage, close date, contact email, and pipeline. Notice the deal stage column. The words in your file must match your stage names exactly. If the file says quote sent, and your stage says quote sent, they will match. If the file says quoted, they will not. This is the number one reason deal imports fail. Our file was prepared to match the new stage names, so we are ready. Go to the deals page, open the add deals menu, and choose import. Click import data, then pick advanced imports. Tick two objects, contacts and deals, because one file will create the deals and link them to people who already exist. For contacts, choose to update existing records only, so the import never creates a duplicate person. Then upload the file. On the mapping screen, check each column. Deal name, amount, deal stage, close date, and pipeline go to deal properties. If a column lands in the wrong place, open its import as menu, and pick deal properties. The contact email column goes to the contact. That is what links each deal to its person. Check every row of the mapping, including pipeline. In an advanced import, HubSpot needs to know which pipeline every deal belongs to. We will check the result at the end, because imports with links are a place where small things go wrong. Name the import Tallgrass deals, choose the legal basis for the contacts, and finish the import. Review the summary. Twenty deals created, twenty associations, and zero errors. That is a clean import. Open the board. You should now see cards spread across the columns. Each card shows the deal name, the amount, and the close date. Let's look at a few. A roof inspection for one hundred ninety nine dollars, already won. A gutter replacement for eighteen hundred dollars, won in October. A shingle repair for six hundred fifty dollars, waiting after inspection. Click one card. You will see the deal record, much like a contact. The preview shows the amount, the close date, the pipeline, and the stage. We will open the full record in a moment. As each job moves forward, your team moves its card to the next column. The stage updates. That simple motion is how your team will use the pipeline every day. Someone finishes an inspection, and the card moves on. At the bottom of each column, HubSpot adds up the value of the deals in it. This is a first look at your money. You can already see how much is waiting at the quote stage, which is often where a business loses track of things. A few cleanup tips. If your deals look wrong after the import, do not panic. On the import summary, you can clean up your import, fix your file, and run it again. This is another reason to keep your original files. Also think about who owns each deal. Every deal has an owner, the person responsible for it. Ours show no owner yet. When you import, you can map an owner column. On a small team, ownership keeps jobs from falling through the cracks. Take a breath. This was the longest step, and it was the most important one. You now have a real pipeline, full of real looking jobs. Next, we tell HubSpot what we sell. Step seven of twelve. Products. Right now, our deals have an amount, but they do not say what was sold. Products fix that. A product is something you sell, saved once, with a name and a price. When you add it to a deal, you do not retype anything. You pick it from a list. Tallgrass sells five services. A roof inspection, for one hundred ninety nine dollars. A shingle repair covering up to one hundred square feet, for six hundred fifty dollars. A gutter replacement, for eighteen hundred dollars. A storm damage repair, for four thousand two hundred dollars. And a full roof replacement, for fourteen thousand five hundred dollars. Open the more menu, then C R M, then products. This is your products library. It is empty for now. Open the add products menu, and choose create a product. Let's make the first one by hand, so you see every field. Name it roof inspection, set the type to service, and the unit price to one hundred ninety nine. For the description, write full roof inspection with photo report. Then click create. For the other four, use an import. Our file has a name, a unit price, and a description for each service. Open add products, choose import, then advanced imports, and products. Upload the file, check the mapping, and name the import Tallgrass services. Finish it. Four new products join the roof inspection. Now all five services are in the library. Check the prices carefully. A typo in a price will follow you into every deal. Now let's use them. Open a deal, the shingle repair for Ashley Alvarez. At first, the record has no line items section. Click customize, add the line items card to the default view, and save. Now the section is there. On the line items card, click add, then select from product library, and pick shingle repair. HubSpot fills in the name and the price, six hundred fifty dollars. You can change the quantity, or add a discount. Keep the quantity at one, and save. The deal amount still says manual, six hundred fifty dollars. It matches the line item, and that is what counts. That means the number on the card matches what you actually plan to charge. You are no longer guessing. Why does this help? Because later you can ask a better question. Which service brings in the most money? Which one do we sell the most often? A simple list of deals cannot answer that. Products can. There is also a lesson here about keeping data honest. If everyone types an amount by hand, you will see slightly different numbers for the same job. If everyone picks a product, the numbers agree. Try adding line items to two or three more deals. Do not feel you must update all twenty right now. Start with the ones that matter, and use products from here on, for every new deal. Your catalog is ready. Now, let's talk about keeping in touch. Step eight of twelve. Tasks and activities. A pipeline shows you where deals are. Activities show you what to do next. This is the part that actually makes you money. Let's start with the simplest activity, logging a call. Open a deal. Let's use the shingle repair for Ashley Alvarez, who is waiting on a quote. On the record, click the activities tab, in the middle of the page. You will see tabs like notes, emails, calls, tasks, and meetings. Open calls, and click log a call. Why log a call, and not call? Placing calls from HubSpot is a paid feature, as that popup showed. Logging a call you made from your phone is free. A box opens. Pick the contact, Ashley, then set the outcome to connected, and the direction to outbound. Write a short note. Called Ashley after the inspection. Two shingles missing on the north side. She wants a quote for the repair this week. Under the note, tick the box to create a follow up task. The default, in three business days, is fine. Then log the activity. Your call is now part of the story, in order. Anyone on your team who opens this record can read it, so no more asking in the group chat what happened last Tuesday. When something matters, write it down in the record, not in your head, and not on a sticky note. Now, a task. A task is a reminder with a due date. Click the task button at the top of the deal. Title it, send quote to Ashley Alvarez. The due date is in two business days, at eight in the morning. That works. Add a reminder one hour before, and set the priority to high. Click create. The task is now attached to the deal. It also shows on your own task list. Open the tasks page from the main menu. If an upgrade offer pops up, close it. You will see all tasks, with quick views for due today, overdue, and upcoming. Here are our two tasks. This page can become your daily to do list. Each morning, open it and start at the top. Here is a good habit. Whenever you finish an activity, ask yourself, what happens next? Then create the next task before you close the record. A deal without a next step is a deal that quietly dies. Tasks work the same way from a contact or a company record. Wherever you create one, it lands on the same task list, so nothing gets lost. Meetings are another type of activity. If you book site visits, you can log them under the meetings tab. You can also connect your email and calendar. We skip it here. It saves typing, but it shares data, so read each permission first. The reminder we set will notify you before the task is due. You can fine tune these alerts later, in your notification settings. Do not turn everything on. Too many alerts and you will ignore them all. Choose the ones that help you act. Finally, notice that every activity is stored on the record. Over time, you build a full history of each customer. When someone calls after two years, you can see what you quoted, what they chose, and what you promised. That history is the real value of a customer relationship manager. It is memory, shared by everyone. Next, let's save you from retyping emails. Step nine of twelve. Email templates. You will send some version of the same message again and again. A quote, a follow up, a thank you. Templates save you from writing them from scratch every time. First, find the templates area. Click the search bar at the top, find in HubSpot, and type templates. Open message templates, and click start from scratch. First, give it a name, your roof quote. Then the subject line. Keep it clear and plain. For example, your roof quote from Tallgrass and Tin Roofing. Now the body. Write it the way you would speak to a neighbor. Start with a greeting. Type hi, and a space. Now comes the first thing to learn about templates. They can pull in details from the record. These are called personalization tokens. Click insert, then personalization tokens. Pick contact, search for first name, and add it. When the email goes out, HubSpot replaces it with the real name. Write the next line. Thanks for having us out to look at your roof. Here is your quote. Then one line per service. Shingle repair, up to one hundred square feet, six hundred fifty dollars. Then the next step. Reply to this email or call us, and we will get you on the schedule. Add a clear closing, with the company name. Tallgrass and Tin Roofing. Keep the whole message short. People read short emails. Now, a few cautions. Always set a fallback for each token. If a contact has no first name saved, the fallback steps in. Set it to the word there. If the name is missing, the email reads, hi there, and not hi blank. This small detail prevents embarrassing mistakes. Preview the template with a real contact. Pick Ashley Alvarez, click generate, and check that her name appears. Read it out loud. If it sounds stiff, loosen it. Now save the template. Its name, your roof quote, says exactly what it is. A clear name helps you find it later. On the free plan, you can keep up to three templates, and the counter shows one of three created. To send it, you need an inbox connected to HubSpot. We skip that in this demo account. In yours, open a contact, click email, choose the template, and add one personal line about their roof. That is the best of both worlds. Fast, and still human. We are using fake addresses in this video, so nothing real will go out. In your own account, you will send to real people. Always double check the recipient before you press send. Think about a few more templates to create over time. A follow up after three days. A thank you after the job. A reminder before an inspection. Build them as the need appears, not all at once. One more thing worth knowing. When you send an email through HubSpot, it logs on the contact timeline automatically, if your email is connected. You will see when it was sent, and in many cases when it was opened. Use that information as a hint, not as proof. An open does not always mean the person read it. Your messages are ready. Now let's make it easy to find the right people. Step ten of twelve. Views and filters. By now, you have a lot of data. Sixty contacts, twenty deals, six companies. Imagine that growing to six hundred, or six thousand. You need a way to see just the slice you care about. That is what filters do. And when you save a filter, it becomes a view. Go to the contacts page. Next to the view tabs, click the plus, and choose create new view. Pick the table layout, and name it customers in Austin. Now open advanced filters. Add a filter, choose city, and pick Austin. Eleven contacts match. Add a second filter. Choose lifecycle stage, and pick customer. Now the table shows only customers in Austin. In our data, that is two people. Both conditions must be true. Look at the count below the table. It tells you how many records match. If it feels wrong, check your filters. A common mistake is spelling a city differently from the data. Now save it. Click save. HubSpot confirms the view was updated. Its name, customers in Austin, stays on the tab. It now appears as a tab above the table. Anyone on your team can click it and see the same list, without rebuilding it. Let's make a second view, this time for deals. Go to the deals page, click the plus next to the tabs, and choose a table. Name it open quotes. Add a filter for the deal stage, and pick two stages, quote sent and quote accepted. Seven deals match. Save it. This one is powerful, because quotes are where follow up matters most. Each Monday, open the view, and call everyone on the list. You can also choose which columns the table shows. Use the option to edit columns, and add the amount and the close date if they are missing. Remove the ones you never look at. A tidy table is easier to scan. You can sort the table too. Click a column header to order by amount, from largest to smallest. This lets you see your biggest opportunities first. Filters can use property values, like our roof type. For example, you could filter your contacts by roof type, metal. You get a list of everyone with a metal roof. If you ran a promotion for metal roofs, that is your audience. A note on limits. The free plan may restrict how many saved views you can keep. If you reach a limit, keep the views you use every week, and delete the rest. Fewer, better views beat a long list nobody opens. Also consider lists. A list is a saved group of contacts that you can use for emails or reports. A view is how you look at records. A list is a group you can act on. For our purposes today, views are enough. You can now find any customer in seconds. Time to see the whole business at once. Step eleven of twelve. Your first dashboard. Everything we have done so far has been about recording data. Now we turn it into answers. Here is the dashboards page. HubSpot already has a default dashboard, called C R M data overview. You can use it, or create your own. Let's create one. Click create dashboard, choose a new dashboard, and name it Tallgrass sales. Next, add reports. The add reports panel opens by itself. HubSpot has many ready made reports. On the free plan, you will have access to a good set of them. Some may be locked behind paid plans, and that is fine. We need only a few. Search for pipeline. The first report to add is deals by stage. It shows how many deals sit at each stage of our pipeline. Add it to the dashboard. You will see a chart, with a slice for each stage. This answers a key question. Where are our jobs right now? The second report is deals by status. It splits your deals into open and won. In our data, it shows four open and two won, this quarter so far. With both added, you have two views side by side. What we might win, and what we have won. Let's look at what the charts tell us. In our data, one job is booked for inspection, two are inspected, and one quote is out. Six quotes are accepted, five jobs are scheduled, and five are already won. The story is easy to read, because the stages are in our own language. Later, you can add a third report. Something about new contacts by lead source. It shows where your customers come from, whether Facebook, Google, or word of mouth. If one source brings the best jobs, spend more time there. You can also arrange the dashboard. Drag the reports into a layout you like. Put the most important at the top left, because that is where your eyes go first. Resize them so the numbers are easy to read. Check the filters at the top of the dashboard. You can set a date range, such as this quarter. You can also filter by owner, to see one person at a time. A word on trust. A dashboard is only as good as the data behind it. If people forget to update stages, the charts will lie. That is why we built simple habits. Drag the card. Log the call. Create the next task. Share the dashboard if you want. You can make it visible to your team, so that everyone sees the same numbers. A weekly look at this page can replace a long status meeting. Here is a routine to try. Every Monday, open the dashboard. Check the pipeline. Then open your open quotes view. Work through your tasks. That ten minute routine is the whole system in action. And that is it. You have built a working customer relationship manager. That brings us to the end. In about forty minutes, we went from an empty account to a business ready to run. Let's look back at what you built. You picked the free plan, and found your way around. You imported sixty contacts, with email as the key that keeps duplicates out. You added six companies, and linked the people to them. You created a custom property for roof type. You built a pipeline that speaks your language, and filled it with twenty deals. You added your products, logged calls, and set tasks. You wrote an email template, saved two views, and built your first dashboard. That is a real system. And you built it step by step, without paying for anything. Now, one honest note. HubSpot changes its screens often. The buttons in your account may sit in a slightly different place. If so, look for the same words, and you will find your way. The ideas stay the same, even when the menus move. What should you do next? Use it. Put in your own contacts, and your own deals. Rename the stages to match how you really work. Do it this week, while the steps are fresh. In the next video, we go deeper into HubSpot for sales. We will look at how to manage your daily work, follow up with more discipline, and turn more quotes into jobs. The link will be in the description. All the sample files from this video are there too, so you can follow along with the same data. If this helped, a like helps others find it. And if you have a question, leave it in the comments. I read them. Thanks for building along. I will see you in the next one.

metadata.title: HubSpot vs Salesforce 2027: Which CRM for SaaS Startups?
metadata.author: VerifiedShortlist
metadata.shortDescription:
HubSpot or Salesforce for your Series A/B SaaS team in 2027? This comparison breaks down the decision around admin capacity, sales motion, customization, AI and total cost.

Building a 5–20 rep sales team? We explain when HubSpot Sales Hub makes sense for an inbound-led team without a dedicated CRM admin, and when Salesforce is a stronger fit for complex workflows and a larger sales organization.

Read the full comparison and FAQ:
https://verifiedshortlist.com/revops/hubspot-vs-salesforce/

In this video:
• Five criteria for choosing your CRM
• HubSpot Sales Hub and Salesforce: strengths and limitations
• Pricing, onboarding fees and cost at your 12-month seat count
• Customization, forecasting and implementation time
• HubSpot Breeze vs Salesforce Agentforce AI
• Marketing-to-sales data, integrations and ecosystem
• Pipedrive, Zoho CRM, Close, Attio, Dynamics 365 Sales and other alternatives

2:07 Salesforce: best fit and limitations
3:13 Pricing and total cost

4:15 HubSpot Breeze vs Salesforce Agentforce AI
4:42 Marketing-to-sales data and integrations
5:10 Alternatives to HubSpot and Salesforce

segments.text: If you're a Series A or B SaaS company
building a 5 to 20 rep sales team, should
your CRM be HubSpot or Salesforce? Here's the short
answer, as of January 2027. Choose HubSpot if you
don't have a dedicated CRM admin and your motion
is inbound-heavy. Choose Salesforce if you expect complex customization,
multiple sales management layers or more than 50 reps.
Both hold the same 4.4 out of 5 on
G2, so this is a fit decision, not a
quality one. Five things decide it. One, admin capacity:
Salesforce's flexibility needs someone to customize it, while HubSpot
mostly works out of the box. Two, marketing-to-sales data:
one platform, or an integration you maintain. Three, total
cost at your 12-month seat count, not the entry
price. Four, AI: ask for a live demo of
your exact workflow, not a slide. Five, ecosystem: Salesforce's
AppExchange lists thousands of apps, and HubSpot's marketplace is
smaller. Get those five right and the choice usually
makes itself. HubSpot Sales Hub is best for Series
A and B sales teams without a dedicated CRM
admin, especially with an inbound-heavy motion, because it shares
one data model with HubSpot's Marketing and Service Hubs.
That means a lead's campaign source, content engagement and
support history sit on the same record your reps
work from. HubSpot has grown to nearly 300,000 paying
customers, and reviewers consistently name ease of use as
its strongest attribute. The free CRM is permanent for
up to two users. Paid plans run Starter at
$20, Professional at $100 plus a $1,500 onboarding fee,
and Enterprise at $150 plus $3,500, per seat per
month. HubSpot holds 4.4 out of 5 across 13,927
G2 reviews, as of January 2027. The limitations: CPQ
and quoting aren't included at any tier, with an
add-on reported at roughly $84 per seat per month,
and reporting is less flexible for complex cross-object scenarios.
Skip HubSpot if you'll need deep customization within 12
months. Salesforce is best for teams expecting complex customization,
multiple sales management layers or more than 50 reps,
because its fully custom data model can represent almost
any business process. Salesforce holds roughly 20% of the
global CRM market by revenue, according to IDC, and
its Sales Cloud was rebranded Agentforce Sales in 2025.
Enterprise Edition adds forecasting across full team hierarchies, and
the AppExchange lists thousands of integrations. Pricing runs Starter
Suite at $25, Pro Suite at $100, Enterprise at
$175, Unlimited at $350 and Agentforce 1 Sales at
$550, per seat per month, billed annually, with a
30-day trial and no free tier. Salesforce holds 4.4
out of 5 across 25,879 G2 reviews, as of
January 2027. The limitations: a real learning curve that
usually needs a dedicated admin or consultant, and no
native marketing automation. Skip Salesforce if you're a 5
to 15 person team with no admin capacity. On
price, the entry tiers are close: HubSpot Starter at
$20 versus Salesforce Starter Suite at $25. The gap
widens at the tiers growing teams actually use. HubSpot
Professional is $100 per seat plus a $1,500 onboarding
fee. Salesforce's realistic floor for real customization, Enterprise, is
$175 per seat. HubSpot Enterprise adds a $3,500 onboarding
fee, and Salesforce Unlimited runs $350. Model the cost
at your 12-month seat count, including add-ons like quoting.
On customization, Salesforce wins: custom objects, validation rules and
page layouts, plus forecasting across team hierarchies. On time
to value, HubSpot wins: standard setups take days to
weeks, while Salesforce takes weeks to months, longer with
heavy customization. Under-resourcing a Salesforce implementation is the most
common regret in buyer discussions, so audit your admin
capacity first. Salesforce's flexibility is a liability without someone
to own it. On AI, both ship agents metered
by usage. HubSpot's Breeze agents, for prospecting, customer and
data tasks, run on HubSpot Credits across Sales Hub
tiers, and HubSpot reports its Prospecting Agent gets up
to 2 times higher response rates. Salesforce's Agentforce is
included with usage limits from Enterprise up, and it's
unmetered only on the $550 Agentforce 1 tier. Ask
both vendors to demo your exact workflow live. On
marketing-to-sales data, HubSpot wins for inbound teams: lead source,
campaign and content engagement flow into the deal record
natively. For an inbound-led startup, that's a structural advantage.
Salesforce needs a separate Marketing Cloud or Account Engagement
purchase. A split stack, HubSpot for marketing and Salesforce
for sales, is common, but it needs an integration
someone maintains. On ecosystem, Salesforce wins if your stack
has tools that only integrate with Salesforce. If neither
fits, the page lists eight more CRMs as an
unranked starting shortlist. A few stand out. Pipedrive for
pipeline-first simplicity, from $24 per seat per month. Zoho
CRM for the most features per dollar, with a
free tier. Close for outbound-heavy SMB teams, with calling
built in. Attio for PLG startups that want custom
objects instead of fixed contacts and deals. And Microsoft
Dynamics 365 Sales if you're standardized on Microsoft. The
page also covers Freshsales, Copper and monday CRM. The
verdict for 2027: it isn't which CRM is better,
it's which one matches your admin capacity. 5 to
15 reps, no admin, inbound-led? Start on HubSpot. Scaling
past 50 reps, with complex data or Salesforce-only tools?
Choose Salesforce. Migrating CRMs later is a real project,
so plan ahead, but don't over-buy for a 60-rep
future you haven't reached yet. The full comparison and
FAQ are on verifiedshortlist.com, linked below.

So those are things that you want to consider and factor in when you're trying to determine how much monthly spend you need to put towards it. But the practice area as well is also going to um make a difference. If you're PI, we know that PI is more expensive. So if we're our PI clients, we don't recommend for any lead generation campaign non-retargeting, so targeting just a cold audience that you spend more than 5,000 a month. The Atlantas, the Houstons, the Los Angeleses, the New York cities of the world are are going to require more budget up front. If you're not in PI, you have a little bit of a lower barrier to entry, which we recommend depending on the practice area starting between 2,500 and 3,000 for a cold lead generation campaign. metadata.title: $4.4B Outreach CEO: The Future of Sales Is AI Agents
metadata.author: Chris Bussing
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode, Abhijit Mitra, CEO of Outreach, shares how the company is using AI agents to transform the way modern sales teams work.

He also shares lessons from his journey building and leading in tech, and his perspective on where the industry is heading.

Check out Outreach →https://www.outreach.ai

Connect With Abhijit →https://www.linkedin.com/in/mitrasaab

Chat with me about 1-1 coaching: 
👉https://calendly.com/bussingventures/session

🏢 Book me for corporate sales training & speaking →https://calendly.com/bussingventures/bussing-sales-speaking-training-consult

🎯 Free Cold Calling System →https://techsalesaccelerator.framer.website/

Timestamps
00:00 - Abhijit’s Outreach origin story
01:32 - Why are companies shifting from software to AI agents?
03:05 - Is Outreach like Jarvis from Iron Man for sales teams?
03:24 - How does Outreach help drive revenue results?
06:10 - The story behind Outreach’s AI agent “Alex”
07:17 - Can AI agents qualify leads while sellers sleep?
08:39 - How does Outreach help expand existing customer revenue?
09:43 - How are companies saving time with Outreach?
12:44 - How does Outreach improve sales forecasting?
13:47 - What excites Abhijit most about the future of Outreach?
14:51 - What does being an underdog mean?
16:05 - Abhijit’s final advice

ABOUT ME:
I help B2B tech companies build world-class outbound sales teams through training programs, workshops, and sales kickoffs. Former seller at Oracle, Google, & an AWS partner who has coached 100s of reps across the industry to hit quota & unlock their personal potential. 
 
»»» Subscribe for weekly tips to help you SELL more and LIVE more! «««

metadata.author: Safe Ozone Energies
metadata.shortDescription:
Lead Scout is an AI-powered sales research and outreach agent built for the Kaggle AI Agents Capstone 2026 (Agents for Business track).
Give it a company name — it researches the company using live web search, drafts a personalized cold outreach email, and logs everything to a CRM tracker for human review. What normally takes a sales rep 20–30 minutes of manual research happens automatically in under a minute.
How it works:
▶ Researcher Agent — searches the web in real time using Google Search to find what the company does, recent news, and likely pain points
▶ Writer Agent — drafts a short, personalized cold email grounded in the research
▶ Saver Agent — logs the result to a CRM tracker (status: PENDING REVIEW — nothing is ever sent automatically)
Built with:

Google Agent Development Kit (ADK) — SequentialAgent orchestrating three sub-agents
Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite
Custom MCP-style tool (save_lead_record)
Streamlit (live deployed UI)
Google Antigravity (test plan generation)

metadata.title: AI Agents in Sales: From Account Research to Proposal (and the One Check That Saves the Deal)
metadata.author: Ambilio
metadata.shortDescription:
How are AI agents used in sales, and where do they get client facts wrong? This AI for sales tutorial follows Olivia Grant, an Account Executive. Her AI agent researches an account, qualifies the lead and drafts the proposal. Then it gets one fact wrong.

In this video you’ll learn:
- Where AI agents fit in the sales cycle, from lead to proposal
- AI account research: the five questions good research answers
- AI lead qualification: evidence behind every score
- AI proposal drafting: the inputs, and the review that matters
- Four ways AI agents get client facts wrong
- Five verification habits for sales teams using AI
- AI sales follow-ups: what the agent can draft, and what it can’t promise

Chapters
0:00 Introduction
0:37 Where AI agents fit in sales
1:53 AI account research
2:43 AI lead qualification
3:38 AI proposal drafting
4:56 Why AI agents get client facts wrong
5:36 Five verification habits
6:39 AI sales follow-ups
7:13 Recap

Incubity by Ambilio builds the capability your sales teams need to work with AI agents, and to check what they produce.
🌐 incubity.ambilio.com

Source: Salesforce, State of Sales report, 2026.

#AIAgents #AIForSales #SalesAI #AgenticAI

So where do AI agents help sales [music]
professionals? Account research, lead

Where do they go wrong? Stale, [music]

metadata.title: How to Build an Email Outreach AI Agent in n8n
metadata.author: AI Automation Official
metadata.shortDescription:
How to build an email outreach AI agent in n8n that writes personalized cold and follow-up emails.

In this video:
• What the outreach agent does
• Why sales teams and freelancers want this
• Basic structure in n8n
• System prompt tips for natural emails
• Key inputs (name, company, research notes)
• What good outreach emails look like
• How to pair it with the lead research agent

Start simple: generate the email and review it. Then expand to sequences.

Subscribe for practical AI automation.

#n8n #AIAgents #EmailOutreach #AIAutomation #Sales

segments.text: We've built lead research and support
agents. Now, let's create another
practical one, an email outreach AI
agent. An email outreach agent helps you
write personalized cold or follow-up
emails at scale. It can take a lead's
name, company, and a few details, then
generate a short, relevant message.
Sales teams and freelancers use this to
save hours of writing. Here's how to
structure it in n8n. Start with a
trigger. This is often a Google Sheet
row, a form, or a webhook that provides
the lead information. Then add an AI
agent node. Connect a language model and
write a clear system prompt. Tell the
agent you write short, personalized
outreach emails. Keep the tone
professional, but friendly. Focus on the
recipient's company or role. Do not
sound salesy or generic. End with a
clear, low-pressure call to action. Give
the agent the key inputs, the person's
name, company, their role if available,
and any research notes. The better the
input, the better the email. You can
also add tools if needed, such as a web
search tool to pull recent company news,
or a tool that sends the email once
approved. For the first version, keep it
simple. Generate the email text and save
it to a spreadsheet or send it to you
for review. Good outreach emails are
short. Aim for four to seven sentences.
Mention something specific about the
company. State the value clearly and ask
one simple question. This agent pairs
well with the lead research agent.
Research first, then generate the
outreach message. You can sell them
together as a full outbound system.
Start by testing with five or 10 real
leads. Improve the prompt until the
emails sound natural, then expand to
automatic sending or multi-step
sequences. In the next video, we can
cover common mistakes or another agent.
Subscribe so you don't miss it. Drop a
comment if you want a sample system
prompt for outreach.

metadata.author: AI for Every Job
metadata.shortDescription:
Follow one deal from first research to renewal and see how salespeople can use AI in 2026 for account research, outreach, call prep, follow-ups and CRM hygiene. You stay in charge of the relationship: AI drafts and summarises, you check every fact and every message before it goes out.

Chapters
0:00 Intro
0:35 Research the account
1:24 The first outreach
2:27 The discovery call
3:24 Follow-up and proposal
4:12 Prep for objections
4:59 Forecast and CRM hygiene
5:55 Handover and renewal
6:38 Three rules
7:20 Wrap-up

Tools mentioned: LinkedIn Sales Navigator (Account IQ, Lead IQ, Message Assist), HubSpot Prospecting Agent, HubSpot Breeze Assistant, Gong (call brief, Gong Assistant, AI Deal Predictor), Salesforce Agentforce Sales Coach, Gemini "Help me write" in Gmail.

AI for Every Job: practical, honest guides to using AI in your profession. Subscribe and tell us in the comments which job we should cover next.

Made with AI tools: the script was researched and written with AI assistance, and the narration and animated presenter are AI-generated.

#AIforSales #SalesTips #AIforEveryJob

segments.text: Selling in 2026 still comes down to
trust between people, but the research
notes follow-ups and admin around every
deal.
AI can carry much of that. So we follow
one deal.
Priya is an account executive selling
scheduling software, and her target is a
regional food distributor we will call
Northfield Foods. From research and
outreach to discovery, proposal,
objections, forecasting, and handover,
real tools, prompts you can copy, honest
limits, and three rules at the end.
It starts before any email.
Priya has an hour to learn who runs
Northfield, what changed recently, and
why they might care about scheduling
now. In LinkedIn Sales Navigator,
Account IQ summarizes an account,
recent activity, key decision makers,
company priorities, and signals like
hiring or leadership changes. A fast
first briefing. Then Lead IQ for the
person. It summarizes a buyer's role and
background and highlights recent news or
shared interests.
Priya reads it on the head of operations
at Northfield. Then she pastes public
notes into an assistant.
Based only on this, give three reasons
this company might need better
scheduling now and what I must confirm.
Now the first message. A generic email
gets ignored. A personal one takes time.
AI drafting helps most here and can also
do the most damage. In HubSpot, the
prospecting agent researches accounts,
finds contacts, and drafts personalized
emails in the rep's voice.
Reps can review and edit each draft
before it is sent. On LinkedIn, Message
Assist in beta drafts a first in mail
using lead and company data and suggests
conversation starters like shared
connections.
Priya rewrites the opening herself. Then
she asks an assistant, list every
factual claim in this email and mark
which ones I could not prove. Anything
invented like a customer result comes
out. More email faster can break rules.
Anti-spam and data protection laws
differ by country, so follow company
policy, respect opt-outs, and never let
volume replace relevance.
Northfield replies and Priya books a
discovery call.
Her job on the call is to listen well,
so AI helps with preparation before and
notes after. Before the call she asks, I
am meeting ahead of operations at a food
distributor. Write 10 open discovery
questions about scheduling pain without
assuming any answers. Her team uses
Gong. After a recorded call, Gong
creates a call brief with what was
discussed and key takeaways plus an
outline with timestamps. She can ask
Gong assistant about the call like list
objections or suggest next steps and
answers cite the conversation. She still
checks key moments herself. Before any
recording, tell everyone and get
consent. Recording laws differ by place,
so check local rules in your company's
policy.
This is general information, not legal
advice.
After discovery, speed matters. A clear
same-day follow-up shows you really
listened. Then comes the proposal which
must be accurate, not just quick. If
Priya works in Gmail, help me write in
Gemini drafts an email from a prompt.
She types, thank Dana for the call,
recap the three problems, propose a
pilot. Then she edits. In HubSpot,
Bree's assistant can refine outreach and
personalize messages using deal context
and customer history from the CRM.
Useful when a deal has months of notes.
For the proposal, using only these call
notes and our approved product sheet,
draft a one-page proposal in the
customer's own words.
Pricing and terms come from her team.
The proposal lands and the finance
director has questions.
Priya does not want to hear tough
objections first on a live call, so she
practices. In Salesforce, Agent for
Sales Coach runs role plays that
simulate a buyer based on the rep's
deal.
Reps practice pitching, objections, and
negotiation, then get feedback after
each session. With any assistant, play a
skeptical finance director at a food
distributor. Push back on cost and
switching risk. After five questions,
tell me where my answers were weak. Then
list what we could offer if they ask for
a discount and what we could ask in
return. She takes that to her manager.
AI suggests people approve.
Every Monday, Priya's manager asks, will
Northfield close this quarter? An honest
answer depends on clean records, the
part of the job sellers like least. She
pastes her latest notes into an approved
assistant. Turn these into CRM fields,
next step, date, decision maker, risks.
Then she checks every field before
saving. Gong's AI deal predictor scores
open deals against the rest of the
pipeline using CRM data, calls, and
emails, and shows positive and negative
signals behind each score. Priya asks an
assistant, based on these deal notes,
what is missing for this to close on
time? It points out she has never spoken
to anyone in procurement.
An AI score is an estimate, only as good
as the data behind it. Treat it as a
prompt for questions, not a promise to
your manager.
Northfield signs, but the deal is not
done. A messy handover can sour a new
customer, and next year's renewal really

metadata.shortDescription:
Get your free personalized $100M scaling roadmap: https://www.acquisition.com/roadmap

If you’re new to my channel, my name is Alex Hormozi. I’m the founder and managing partner of Acquisition.com. It’s a family office, which is just a formal way of saying we invest our own money into companies. Our 10 portfolio companies bring in over $250,000,000+ per year. Our ownership stake varies between 20% and 100% of them. Given this is a YT channel, and anyone can claim anything, I’ll give you some stuff you can google to verify below.

How I got here…

21: Graduated Vanderbilt in 3 years Magna Cum Laude, and took a fancy consulting job.
23 yrs old: Left my fancy consulting job to start a business (a gym).
24 yrs old: Opened 5 gym locations.
26 yrs old: Closed down 6th gym. Lost everything. 
26 yrs old: Got back to launching gyms (launched 33). Then, lost everything for a 2nd time. 
26 yrs old: In desperation, started licensing model as a hail mary. It worked. 
27 yrs old: "Gym Launch" does $3M profit the next 6 months. Then $17M profit next 12 months.
28 yrs old: Started Prestige Labs. $20M the first year.  
29 yrs old: Launched ALAN, a software company for agencies to work leads for customers. Scaled to $1.7mmo within 6 months. 
31 yrs old: Sold 75% of UseAlan to a strategic buyer in an all stock deal. 
31 yrs old: Sold 66% of Gym Launch & Prestige Labs at $46.2M valuation in all-cash deal to American Pacific Group. (you can google it)
31 yrs old: Started our family office Acquisition.com. We invest and scale companies using the $42M in distributions we had taken + the cash from the $46.2M exit.
32 yrs old: Started making free content showing how we grow companies to make real business education accessible to everyone (and) to attract business owners to invest or scale their businesses. 
34 yrs old: I became co-owner of https://Skool.com, which is a platform for people to build communities online, making a living doing what they love, with people like them.
36 yrs old: I did a $106M book launch selling 3.6M copies of my $100M Money Models book, in 72 hours, breaking the Guinness world record for the fastest selling non-fiction book of all time.

Today: Our portfolio now does $200M/yr between 10 companies. The largest doing $100M/yr the smallest doing $5M per year. Our ownership varies between 20% and 100% ownership of the companies. Many of them we invested in early and helped grow (which is how we make our money - not youtube videos).

To all the gladiators in the arena, we’re all in the middle of writing our own stories. The worse the monsters, the more epic the story.

You either get an epic outcome or an epic story. Both mean you win. 

Keep crushing. May your desires be greater than your obstacles. 

Never quit,

Alex

DISCLOSURE 
Information shared here is for educational purposes only.  Individuals and business owners should evaluate their own business strategies, and identify any potential risks.  The information shared here is not a guarantee of success. Your results may vary.
Copyright © 2026.
