metadata.title: How to Generate Enterprise B2B Leads When Sales Cycles Take 6–18 Months
metadata.author: reachmarketingllc
metadata.shortDescription:
Enterprise B2B lead generation for longer sales cycles is the process of attracting, qualifying, and nurturing high-value prospects through complex buying journeys that involve multiple stakeholders and can take 6–18 months to close. 🚀 In this video, we break down exactly how to build a pipeline that survives long deal cycles instead of stalling out.
Enterprise deals don't move fast — they require sign-off from entire buying committees, dozens of touchpoints, and clear proof of ROI before anyone commits. We cover the strategies that keep leads engaged from first touch to closed-won, including:
• Long-term lead nurturing (drip email, newsletters, and value-driven content)
• Multi-touch attribution to see what actually drives decisions
• Demonstrating ROI early with case studies and ROI calculators
• Account-based marketing (ABM) for multi-stakeholder accounts
• Aligning sales and marketing to shorten the cycle and lift conversion rates 📈
Whether you're in SaaS, IT, financial services, or any high-consideration industry, you'll walk away knowing how to turn long, complicated buyer journeys into predictable revenue.
👉 Read the full article here: https://reachmarketing.com/blog/enterprise-b2b-lead-generation-for-longer-sales-cycles/

Common questions answered in this video:
What is enterprise B2B lead generation? How do you generate leads for long sales cycles? Why are enterprise sales cycles so long? How do you nurture B2B leads over months? What is account-based marketing?
#B2BLeadGeneration #EnterpriseSales #LeadGen #ABM #B2BMarketing #SalesCycle #DemandGeneration

A few notes on why it's structured this way: the description opens with a one-sentence direct answer to the core query (which is what answer engines and AI overviews tend to extract), front-loads the target keyword phrase for SEO, and includes a natural-language FAQ block at the bottom to capture "how/what/why" voice and AI search queries. I kept it to two emojis in the body as you asked, plus one in the title.

segments.text: There is a persistent misconception in
B2B marketing. The idea that enterprise
lead generation is just a faster, larger
version of standard consumer lead
capture. We often picture a single
isolated prospect dropping smoothly down
a frictionless vertical funnel. Standard
lead generation is built around
capturing these individual contacts,
usually by optimizing for simple form
fills. The reality of enterprise growth
requires a different model. The core
unit of analysis shifts from an
individual person to a multi-layered
account level buying committee. When an
entire organization tries to navigate a
standard funnel, the nodes get stuck,
branch outward, and loop backward
against the walls. This creates
significant pipeline risk. Longer sales
cycles present opportunities for selling
organizations to misread early
individual research as late-stage
account readiness. A single contact
researching options does not mean the
account is ready to buy. Momentum breaks
when budget cycles fail to align with
marketing engagement, internal
priorities shift, or legal and
procurement departments enter the
process months after the initial
inquiry. Solving this requires
transitioning to a five-layer enterprise
revenue system, an operational framework
designed to measure account progression
rather than individual lead volume. In
enterprise sales, consensus matters more
than individual enthusiasm. Because
these decisions require a group to move
in lockstep, the system's primary role
is to reduce the organizational risk
that keeps these stakeholders from
reaching a collective agreement. Layer
one of the system is account selection.
A functional revenue system begins
before campaign execution by
mathematically constraining the target
universe to prevent resource dilution.
Filtering the market by strict criteria,
company size, regulatory environment,
current technology stack, and known
operational complexities. Tier one
accounts are isolated for highly
personalized one-to-one executive
engagement. Tier 3 accounts, conversely,
receive broader demand generation
programs until stronger intent appears.
Once an account is selected, layer two
is stakeholder mapping. The monolith of
the lead must be fractured into its
component decision makers. These
distinct roles have conflicting
priorities. The executive sponsor
strictly evaluates the purchase based on
business impact and overall strategic
fit. The technical evaluator evaluates
the exact same product, but their
priorities are entirely focused on
integration specifications, reliability,
and data security. Meanwhile, finance
and procurement approach the evaluation
through a lens of vendor risk,
compliance terms, and strict cost
control. A single piece of marketing
collateral or a standardized follow-up
sequence cannot satisfy these
contradictory demands simultaneously.
Building a strategy around a single
contact provides a dangerously
incomplete view of the opportunity.
Stakeholder mapping is the mandatory
prerequisite for advancing the deal.
Layer three is signal interpretation.
Intent data is highly ambiguous on its
own. It only becomes actionable when
interpreted through the lens of the
complete buying group. A low-quality
signal often misleads sales teams. If a
single contact makes a one-time visit to
broad educational category research,
immediate outreach wastes capable senior
and technical roles from the exact same
company engaging in parallel with
pricing and competitor comparison pages.
Capturing these varied signals requires
a multi-channel strategy. Organic search
naturally captures technical evaluators,
while LinkedIn allows for targeted
role-specific executive messaging. Layer
four introduces proof content. The sheer
length of enterprise sales cycles
requires vendors to deliver hard,
verifiable proof much earlier in the
buyer's journey.
The exact purpose of proof content is
empowerment. It provides internal
champions the documentation they need to
build confidence and defend a vendor
recommendation inside their company
before sales is present. This requires
specific formats, technical
documentation, ROI frameworks without
exaggerated claims, and comparison pages
clarifying tradeoffs.
Proof-driven content is not engineered
to generate top-of-funnel awareness. Its
function is to systematically reduce
organizational uncertainty, keeping
target accounts progressing during the
months they avoid direct sales contact.
Applying traditional individual lead
scoring to a complex enterprise context
reveals a fundamental mechanical
mismatch in the system. Assigning
arbitrary points to individual actions,
like opening an email newsletter or
downloading a PDF guide, completely
ignores the reality of account-level
momentum. The required replacement
system is buying group scoring. This
gauge only advances when multiple
distinct stakeholder nodes register
simultaneous engagement. This system
evaluates the aggregate number of
engaged contacts within the target
organization, their specific seniority,
and the recency of their interactions.
This mechanical constraint prevents a
common error, over-prioritizing a highly
active individual at an account that
lacks the budget or architectural fit.
It also prevents the opposite error,
under-prioritizing a high-fit account
where multiple stakeholders are quietly
researching but haven't formally
requested a demo.
Moving to buying group scoring reveals
true account readiness. It protects
expensive sales capacity from presenting
dead-end inquiries.
Layer five is measurement. Relying on
short-term lead volume is a deceptive
practice. It makes enterprise marketing
performance look artificially strong
while hiding pipeline decay.
Single source attribution fails in long
sales cycles. Buyers consume content
months before taking a meeting and
branded search often appears at the very
end of the evaluation process masking
the earlier touch points.
Looking at this dashboard, the rigorous
metrics required to replace lead volume
become clear. Target account engagement
rate, buying group coverage, and sales
accepted account rate. The ultimate goal
of enterprise is directional
understanding of what moves accounts
toward opportunity creation. It is not
about assigning perfect credit for a
specific click.
Constructing a resilient enterprise
revenue system requires completely
abandoning the individual lead as the
primary unit of measurement. Success
depends entirely on the systematic
progression of buying group readiness.

In this video, I sit down with Casey Patterson, Director of NoAM ABM at Snowflake, to break down what ABM actually is and how to run it. We talk account selection, sales alignment, how to think about targeting the right number of accounts, and what authentic AI-powered ABM could look like. We also get into finding mentors, the future of marketing jobs, and how AI is changing the way marketers work day to day.

Join 50,000 people who get Dave's Newsletter here: https://www.exitfive.com/newsletter

metadata.title: I Sourced a $50 Million M&A Deal Using AI!
metadata.author: Willem
metadata.shortDescription:
Discover how I used artificial intelligence to source a $50M off-market M&A deal, revolutionizing how deals are originated in investment banking and private equity. In this video, I break down the exact AI-driven process that allowed me to automate company research, craft hyper-personalized outreach, and outcompete other investment bankers and private equity firms in a crowded market.

You’ll learn:

- How AI automates company research, saving countless hours.
- The power of personalized outreach to engage decision-makers more effectively.
- Why AI provides infinite scalability, helping you identify and pursue more deals than ever before.
- How this strategy can help you stay ahead of the competition and close high-value transactions faster.

Whether you’re an investment banker, private equity professional, or dealmaker, this video will show you how AI can transform your M&A deal origination process and drive unparalleled results.

Don’t forget to like, subscribe, and comment if you found this valuable, and let me know how you’re using AI in your deal sourcing process!

Don’t forget to like, subscribe, and comment if you found this valuable!

My links 🔗
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/willem-westra-...
WW Capital Group: https://wwcapitalgroup.com/
Book a call: https://calendly.com/willem-jma/introcall 
Email: Willem@wwcapitalgroup.com

About me: I'm Willem, CEO of WW Capital Group and Managing Partner of O7Capital Group. I specialize in buy-side M&A and capital raising and I've helped the leading financial firms and private businesses to overcome the toughest challenges in deal origination and capital raising. By combining proven strategies with advanced AI technology, I've created tailored systems that enable my clients to close more transactions, no matter the market conditions, industry competition, or deal size. I post new useful M&A, capital raising, and AI content weekly.

#artificialintelligence  #M&A #dealorigination  #privateequity  #investmentbanking  #aiforbusiness #offmarketdeals #dealsourcing #mergersandacquisitions #aiagents #corporatefinance

metadata.title: The Secrets to Sourcing Proprietary Deals in Private Equity with Ryan Gable
metadata.author: M&A Science
metadata.shortDescription:
🔹 Ryan Gable, Managing Partner, BW Forsyth Partners

Ryan discusses how his team uses a hybrid private equity model backed by Barry-Wehmiller to execute people-first, long-term acquisitions. With over 55 deals and zero exits, Forsyth has developed a sourcing and integration playbook that challenges traditional PE norms, focusing instead on trust, cultural alignment, and multi-decade value creation.

Ryan breaks down how to build relationships that convert to proprietary deal flow, structure rollover equity with flexibility, and align seller incentives for lasting outcomes.

💡 Things you will learn:
🔹 How to source proprietary deals by building trust with founders and prioritizing cultural fit
🔹 Why Forsyth avoids traditional PE norms like over-leveraging and fixed exit timelines
🔹 How they structure flexible equity rollovers and provide liquidity without needing to sell
_____________
💡 Episode Timestamps

[00:02:00] From Investment Banking to Building Forsyth with Barry-Wehmiller
[00:07:00] Why Barry-Wehmiller Created a New Investment Arm Instead of Scaling Internally
[00:10:00] The Hybrid Equity Model: Strategic Backing + PE Agility
[00:14:30] Rollover Equity and How Forsyth Structures Flexible Liquidity
[00:23:30] From Auction Fatigue to Sourcing Proprietary Deals
[00:26:00] How Forsyth Builds Trust With Sellers (And Wins Deals Off-Market)
[00:31:00] Why Founders Should Think About Selling Before They’re Ready to Retire
[00:41:00] Structuring Earnouts that Sellers Actually Want to Hit
[00:49:00] The “Less is More” Approach to Post-Close Integration
[00:56:00] The Future of M&A: Return Expectations, Capital Saturation, and Deal Discipline

I'm your host Kison Patel, founder and CEO of DealRoom and chief scientist at M&A Science. Today I'm joined by Ryan Gable, managing partner at BW Forsyth Partners, a St. Louis based investment firm backed by Barry Wehmiller. Ryan co-founded BW Forsyth in 2009 with a unique approach that blends elements of private equity, family office investing, and strategic M&A. Since then, his team has completed over 55 acquisitions and built seven platform companies across capital equipment, manufacturing, and insurance services. metadata.title: M&A success fees: what does your adviser really cost?
metadata.author: Saverio Canepa
metadata.shortDescription:
Two proposals both quote a 2% success fee. Why can the total bill be different?

In this video, I compare the fee basis, retainer and payment timing through a wholly hypothetical example:
• enterprise value of €10 million and net financial debt of €2 million: equity value of €8 million, with no other adjustments;
• proposal A: 2% of equity value, a €20,000 retainer credited in full, total cost of €160,000 and balance of €140,000;
• proposal B: 2% of enterprise value, an additional €20,000 retainer, total cost of €220,000 and balance of €200,000;
• a €60,000 difference: €40,000 from the wider fee basis and €20,000 from the uncredited retainer.

metadata.title: Business Broker vs M&A Advisor vs Investment Banker: Which Advisor Do You Actually Need?
metadata.author: Exit On Your Terms
metadata.shortDescription:
Choosing between a business broker, an M&A advisor, or an investment banker to sell your company comes down to deal size, buyer access, fees, and licensing.

Not sure which one fits your business? Use the free exit planning tools at https://exitonyourterms.com/tools.

What's the difference between a business broker, an M&A advisor, and an investment banker? Business brokers typically sell smaller Main Street companies (owner earnings usually under $1 million) in asset sales, marketing them through blind ads and buyer databases. M&A advisors handle more complex sales, often $1–5 million+ in EBITDA, going to private equity groups, strategic buyers, and wealthy individuals or families. Investment banks generally start around $10–20 million in EBITDA and up. Hiring the wrong one for your size can cost you upfront fees and the right buyers.

In this video you'll learn:
• What does a business broker do, and which businesses do they sell?
• When does it make sense to hire an M&A advisor?
• Why a structured auction process can backfire for smaller companies
• How much brokers, M&A advisors, and investment bankers charge
• How each type of intermediary is licensed (real estate vs FINRA/SEC)
• Why access to the right buyer pool matters more than prestige

FAQ
Q: Do I need an investment banker to sell my small business?
A: Usually not. Investment banks typically work on much larger deals, and their fees and buyer networks aren't built for small companies.

Q: How are business brokers paid?
A: Mostly at closing, as a percentage of the sale price that often steps down as the price rises (for example, 10% of the first million, 8% of the second, 6% of the third).

Q: Do M&A advisors charge upfront fees?
A: Many do, such as a retainer, valuation, or market assessment fee (often $5,000–$15,000), and sometimes a monthly work fee credited back at closing.

Michael Wildeveld of Exit On Your Terms draws on 24 years of sell-side M&A experience to help business owners plan their exit. This video is for owners comparing sell-side intermediaries before a business sale, whether a Main Street business or a lower middle market company sold to private equity, strategic, or family office buyers.

This video is educational and not financial or legal advice.

Chapters

0:26 - What Does a Business Broker Do?
1:47 - What Does an M&A Advisor Do?
2:38 - The Auction Problem for Smaller Companies
4:14 - When Do You Need an Investment Banker?
4:44 - How Much Do Brokers, Advisors and Bankers Charge?
7:01 - Differences in Licensing
7:45 - Who Can Actually Reach Your Buyers?
10:24 - Choosing the Right Fit Advisor
10:50 - Free Exit Planning Tools

metadata.title: Earn-outs in M&A: three rules to agree before signing
metadata.author: Saverio Canepa
metadata.shortDescription:
An earn-out of up to €4 million: how much will you actually receive? In the same business case, one formula can produce €4 million and another €3.2 million. The cap is identical; the rules are different.

In this video, I explain three points to agree before signing an M&A transaction:
1. The metric: measurement period, business scope, accounting policies and payment formula.
2. Decision-making powers: who controls pricing, resources, integration costs and group charges.
3. Verification and payment: reporting, records, deadlines, disagreements and payment security.

The example compares two alternative formulas for the same year and business, with the upfront price unchanged. Revenue is €11 million against a €10 million target. EBITDA is €1.6 million against a €2 million target. With proportional payment, no minimum threshold and a 100% cap, the earn-out is €4 million or €3.2 million respectively: an €800,000 difference.

These are alternatives, not amounts to add together. The case and formula are illustrative, not a standard contractual mechanism. No metric is always better, and the agreed maximum is not a guaranteed payment.

CHAPTERS
00:00 The cap and the actual payment
00:19 Earn-out versus fixed deferred price
00:37 The assumptions in our example
01:10 Revenue or EBITDA: an €800k difference
01:40 First rule: define the metric
02:00 Second rule: clarify decision-making powers
02:24 Third rule: verification and payment
02:48 Three questions before signing

Video and full guide on my website:
https://saveriocanepa.it/en/podcast/earn-outs/

FURTHER READING
Earn-outs: metrics, control and payment risk
https://saveriocanepa.it/en/earn-out-clauses-practical-guide-ma-mistakes/

Earn-outs: comparing metrics and clauses on the same case
https://saveriocanepa.it/en/italian-earn-outs-interest-alignment-or-tax-trick/

Saverio Canepa | M&A · Executive · AI Strategy

you actually receive?
In the same business case, one formula
can produce 4 million euros, another 3
million 200,000.
The maximum is identical. What changes
is the set of rules that turns
performance into a payment. An earnout
is part of the purchase price linked to
future results or conditions. It can
help bridge the expectations of buyer
and seller. It differs from a fixed
price simply paid later. With an
earnout, the amount itself depends on
the agreed conditions. Consider a
hypothetical example. We compare two
alternative formulas for the same year
and business activities, keeping the
upfront price unchanged. The maximum
earnout is 4 million euros. Payment
increases in proportion to performance
against the target with no minimum
achievement threshold and a cap at 100%.
Revenue is 11 million euros against a
target of 10 million. EBITDA is 1
million 600,000 euros against a target
of 2 million.
Under the revenue formula, performance
exceeds the target. The cap applies and
the payment is 4 million euros. Under
the EBITDA formula, performance reaches
80% of the target. The payment is 3
million 200,000.
A difference of 800,000 euros. These are
alternatives, not two payments to add
together. This formula is an assumption
for our example, not a standard
contractual mechanism. First rule,
define the metric. Revenue alone does
not measure profitability. EBITDA
requires rules on costs, adjustments,
and the scope of the business. Specify
the measurement period, accounting
policies, and payment formula. No metric
is always better. It must fit the
business plan. Second rule, clarify who
can influence performance. After the
sale, who decides pricing, resources,
and integration costs?
Which group costs will be charged to the
business?
Agree operating rules that fit the
business plan and specify how decisions
affecting the calculation will be
treated. Staying with the business does
not by itself guarantee control.
Third rule, make the calculation
verifiable and agree the payment terms.
This requires regular reporting, access
to records, deadlines, and a procedure
for resolving disagreements.
Clarify who must pay and what payment
security is available. A guarantee can
reduce the risk of non-payment. It
cannot ensure that performance targets
are achieved. Before signing, ask, "What
are we measuring? Who can influence
performance? How do we verify it? And
when do we get paid?"
A well-designed earnout connects
targets, decision-making powers, and
payment terms.
And the conditional future amount needs
to be assessed separately from cash
received today.
You will find the example and further
analysis on my website.
